sentences: Parallel repetition tries to reduce the success probability of a game by asking players to win many independent instances simultaneously.
Entangled players can correlate their strategies across instances, making this amplification harder to analyze than independent play suggests.
The extracted passage describes the historical question of whether a game with entangled value below one could retain a success probability bounded away from zero under arbitrarily many repetitions.
The same paper then rules out that behavior for the setting it studies, while distinguishing this result from stronger quantitative decay claims and transformations of the game.
This entry therefore introduces a source-resolved question and the surrounding amplification issue rather than treating the quoted historical uncertainty as a fresh unresolved claim.
working_summary.note: The quoted introductory question is answered in the same paper; quantitative decay and modified-game variants must be distinguished.

cards.title: Do some tautologies require superpolynomial Extended Frege proofs?
cards.formal: Is Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every constants C>0 and c≥1, is there a propositional tautology φ whose shortest Extended Frege proof has bit length greater than C(|φ|+2)ᶜ? Here |φ| is the bit length of the explicitly written formula.
cards.definitions: Fix Boolean formulas over ¬ and →, with → interpreted as material implication and variable indices encoded in binary. Use the Frege axiom schemes A→(B→A), (A→(B→C))→((A→B)→(A→C)), and (¬B→¬A)→(A→B), together with modus ponens from A and A→B to B. An Extended Frege proof of φ may additionally introduce an abbreviation variable e by the two extension axioms e→θ and θ→e. Here e is fresh, absent from φ, θ, and every preceding line; θ uses original variables of φ and previously introduced extension variables. Extensions are thus acyclic definitions. Other proof lines are axiom instances or applications of modus ponens, and the last line must be φ, with no extension variables. Lines may cite and reuse earlier lines arbitrarily: proofs are not required to be trees. Proof size is the full binary encoding length of all explicitly written formulas, extension definitions, and inference references; there is no depth or per-line-size restriction. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. This fixed presentation is polynomially equivalent to the usual Extended Frege systems, so changing a standard finite Frege basis does not change polynomial boundedness. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Extended Frege captures a powerful form of efficient propositional reasoning with reusable definitions. A superpolynomial lower bound would cross one of the central barriers in proof complexity and clarify whether a standard, highly expressive certificate language necessarily fails on some short true statements.

importance.reason: A defining open lower-bound problem for strong propositional reasoning, closely connected to bounded arithmetic, circuit complexity, and the limits of efficiently checkable certificates.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow formalize propositional proof systems, polynomial simulation, and Extended Frege, proving robustness under the choice of standard rules and connectives.
Strong lower bounds emerge for weaker systems, while even unrestricted Frege lower bounds remain open. EF adds the ability to abbreviate and share formulas.

Pich and Santhanam establish conditional routes from EF proof lower bounds to P≠NP. The assumptions include formally provable computational statements; the result is not an unconditional EF lower bound.
Hsieh, Jain, Li, and Mathialagan obtain SNARGs for NP from derandomization, LWE, SXDH, and a bounded-arithmetic unprovability assumption concerning certificates of EF-hard tautologies.

Alekseev’s journal paper proves an exponential bit-size lower bound for algebraic Binary Value Principle refutations in extended polynomial calculus with a square-root rule. Its Section 1 explicitly distinguishes this from propositional Frege and EF lower bounds.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the primary proof-complexity sources, including Alekseev’s June 2026 journal article. Research through 10 September 2026 found no unconditional resolution for unrestricted Extended Frege. The algebraic and conditional results cited here retain their stated scope.

context_blocks.text: Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If NP≠coNP, every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of NP≠coNP.

Recent algebraic lower bounds illustrate an encoding issue. Alekseev proves exponential bit-size lower bounds for an extension of polynomial calculus that can simulate EF on suitable propositional translations. The hard Binary Value Principle instance is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size CNF. The paper explicitly explains that its result therefore does not yield a Frege or EF lower bound.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to P≠NP under additional bounded-arithmetic assumptions. This explores the consequences of proof-complexity hypotheses without proving an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh and coauthors construct succinct arguments under derandomization, cryptographic, and formal unprovability assumptions. Their result connects the difficulty of certifying hard tautologies to cryptography; it does not establish the unconditional size lower bound asked for here.

cards.title: Does Frege simulate Extended Frege with polynomial proof size?
cards.formal: Do there exist constants C>0 and k≥1 such that every Extended Frege proof π of a propositional tautology φ has some ordinary Frege proof ρ of the same formula with |ρ|≤C(|π|+2)ᵏ? Equivalently, if sF(φ) and sEF(φ) are the minimum proof sizes in the two systems, is sF(φ) polynomially bounded in sEF(φ), uniformly over all tautologies?
cards.definitions: Fix formulas over negation ¬ and material implication →, with binary-encoded variable indices. Ordinary Frege uses the axiom schemes A→(B→A), (A→(B→C))→((A→B)→(A→C)), and (¬B→¬A)→(A→B), and modus ponens: infer B from A and A→B. A proof is a finite sequence ending with φ; earlier lines may be cited and reused without restriction. Extended Frege adds acyclic definitions, introducing the pair e→θ and θ→e, where e is a new variable absent from φ, θ and all preceding lines. θ may use variables of φ and earlier extension variables. The final formula contains no extension variables. Proof size is the complete binary encoding length of every explicitly written line, definition and inference reference. No formula-depth, proof-depth or tree-shape bound is imposed. These presentations are polynomially equivalent to the usual finite-basis Frege and Extended Frege systems. The target is existence of short translated proofs: it does not require a polynomial-time function that finds ρ from π. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This asks whether reusable definitions fundamentally shorten mathematical proofs, beyond any polynomial factor. It is one of the central comparisons between strong propositional proof systems and captures the difficulty of reasoning with shared circuits versus explicit formulas.

importance.reason: A canonical strong-system simulation problem, directly tied to Frege lower bounds, finite consistency and circuit-based reasoning.

progress.text: Cook–Reckhow’s framework establishes the robustness of standard Frege and Extended Frege presentations; EF contains ordinary Frege.
Buss characterizes the simulation by polynomial-size Frege proofs of partial EF consistency statements.
Buss’s mini-tutorial explicitly identifies Frege versus EF as a longstanding open simulation question.
Aisenberg and coauthors obtain polynomial EF and quasipolynomial Frege upper bounds for Kneser–Lovász principles, without proving a lower-bound separation.
Krajíček gives an EF/circuit-equivalence rewriting characterization, retaining circuit intermediate representations.
ECCC TR26-166 extends quasipolynomial Frege simulation to two-group partially commutative formula IPS over GF(2).

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No polynomial size simulation or superpolynomial separation of unrestricted Frege and EF was found in the primary literature. The newest checked simulation, TR26-166, concerns a restricted algebraic formula system and has quasipolynomial overhead.

context_blocks.text: The extension rule gives reusable names to intermediate computations. If a subformula is used many times, ordinary formula syntax writes out each occurrence; Extended Frege can define it once and refer to its name. A network of such definitions represents a Boolean circuit with shared gates. The rule does not permit a false final theorem: every assignment to the original variables uniquely extends through the definitions, and the conclusion uses only original variables.

Repeated substitution eliminates definitions, but can create exponentially large formula trees. This explains why the obvious simulation is expensive; it does not prove that all ordinary Frege proofs must be expensive. The challenge is to compare the shortest proofs, not one syntactic expansion procedure.

The distinction between proof size and proof-search time is essential. The quantifiers are “for every EF proof there exists a short Frege proof.” They do not supply an algorithm for locating that proof. The stronger notion usually called p-simulation requires a polynomial-time transformation. A size simulation alone can hold even if the available methods for finding the translated proof are much slower.

Buss connects the comparison to finite consistency statements. Frege has polynomial-size proofs of its own partial consistency, meaning the corresponding finite statements that no contradiction has a proof up to a specified length. His theorem characterizes Frege simulation of EF by polynomial-size Frege proofs of the analogous partial consistency statements for EF. This turns a comparison of all proofs into a canonical family of propositional statements; it is not a general proof of the desired simulation.

For example, Aisenberg and coauthors give polynomial-size EF proofs and quasipolynomial-size Frege proofs of propositional Kneser–Lovász coloring principles. That upper bound constrains possible lower bounds for the family, but it does not demonstrate a separation and does not rule out a polynomial Frege upper bound. Quasipolynomial and polynomial must remain distinct in this problem.

Krajíček’s June 2026 paper gives a circuit-rewriting description of EF reasoning. An EF proof of circuit equivalence yields a polynomially long chain of equivalence-preserving rewrites; each rewrite adds at most seven gates and may delete gates. This is a normal-form result about circuit reasoning. The intermediate objects still retain circuit sharing, so it does not turn an arbitrary EF proof into a polynomial-size formula-based Frege proof.

A September 2026 preprint by Chatterjee, Chatterjee, Ghosal and Mukhopadhyay proves a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a partially commutative formula version of the Ideal Proof System over GF(2). Variables lie in two groups: they commute across groups but not within a group. The proof formalizes an identity-testing algorithm inside Frege. The restrictions on the algebraic certificates, and the quasipolynomial overhead, both matter; the theorem is not the full EF simulation asked for here.

A negative answer would establish a concrete benefit of reusable definitions for strong propositional reasoning. It would also imply superpolynomial Frege lower bounds, since the final formula is part of every EF proof. By contrast, proving that Frege has some hard tautologies, or assuming NP≠coNP, does not automatically separate it from EF: those same tautologies might require equally long EF proofs. The separate question of whether EF itself is polynomially bounded asks about a different comparison.

cards.title: Superpolynomial AC⁰[p]-Frege lower bounds
cards.formal: For every fixed prime p, does there exist a family of propositional tautologies (τ_{p,n})_{n≥1}, constructible in time polynomial in n, whose encoded lengths lie between n and n^O(1), such that each τ_{p,n} is a DNF and, for every fixed proof-line depth d and every constant r>0, infinitely many n have the following property: every depth-at-most-d Frege proof with MOD_p connectives of τ_{p,n} has total encoded size greater than n^r? The proof system and depth convention are specified below; the family may depend on p but not on d or r.
cards.definitions: A tautology evaluates to true on every Boolean assignment. A DNF is a disjunction of conjunctions of literals, with a literal being a variable or its negation. Fix a conventional sound, implicationally complete finite Frege calculus F over constants 0,1 and connectives NOT, AND, OR. A proof is a sequence of formulas, each a substitution instance of an axiom or obtained from earlier lines by a rule of F; earlier lines may be reused arbitrarily. Extend the language and rules as F(MOD_p) in Krajíček §5: MOD_{p,j}(A_1,…,A_t) is true precisely when the number of true arguments is j modulo p, for 0≤j<p. Besides F’s rules with formulas from this language, permit the empty-list axioms MOD_{p,0}() and NOT MOD_{p,j}() for j≠0, and all instances of MOD_{p,j}(Γ,A) ↔ [(MOD_{p,j}(Γ) AND NOT A) OR (MOD_{p,j−1}(Γ) AND A)], with j−1 taken modulo p and Γ any list of formulas. Constants and variables have depth zero; NOT and MOD increase depth by one, while consecutive ANDs, or consecutive ORs, are flattened and together count as one layer. Every line, including instantiated axioms, obeys the bound d. Proof size counts all symbols and encoded variable indices across all lines, together with rule annotations. Proofs are ordinary Frege proofs, without extension-variable definition axioms; they need not be tree-like or have bounded derivation-graph depth. Standard choices of F give equivalent systems up to polynomial overhead and a constant depth adjustment, immaterial when every fixed d is quantified.
cards.answer_criterion: Exhibit the uniform tautology families and prove the stated superpolynomial proof-size lower bounds, or refute their existence. The tautology condition must itself be established: a formula that has no short proof because it is false is not a hard tautology. A lower bound only for bounded derivation depth, regular proofs, a restricted algebraic subsystem or Boolean circuits alone does not settle this question. A result for one prime is a major partial answer; this single card groups the full fixed-prime frontier rather than duplicating it for each modulus.
cards.why: A central frontier in propositional proof complexity: current methods can handle ordinary bounded-depth reasoning but still cannot establish explicit superpolynomial lower bounds once modular counting is available. The problem tests how circuit lower-bound ideas can constrain entire deductions.

importance.reason: A classical next step beyond the strongest broadly established bounded-depth Frege lower bounds, with direct connections to algebraic proof systems and a persistent gap between circuit and proof complexity.

progress.text: Ajtai establishes superpolynomial bounded-depth Frege lower bounds for the pigeonhole principle; Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo’s 1993 paper gives exponential improvements. These systems lack MOD_p gates.
Krajíček develops extended Nullstellensatz systems and explains their connection to modular Frege lower bounds; §5 fixes the proof-system presentation used here.
Efremenko and Itsykson publish amortized-closure lifting and stronger size-versus-derivation-depth results for resolution over parities.
Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret publish their no-short-proof result for candidate DNFs, first posted in September 2025; unconditional tautologicity remains open.
Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov give near-quadratic-depth lifting and a quadratic unconditional size lower bound for parity resolution. These do not settle general modular Frege.
Hakoniemi, Limaye and Tzameret release hard CNF instances for the read-once-oblivious algebraic-branching-program fragment of IPS.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The 2026 primary sources retain modular Frege lower bounds as open. ITCS 2026.99 does not prove that its hard-to-prove candidates are tautologies. ECCC TR26-018 restricts derivation depth or proves a polynomial size bound; TR26-070 treats a restricted algebraic certificate representation. None establishes the fully specified tautology families and unrestricted derivation size lower bounds requested here.

context_blocks.text: Proof complexity measures how long a formal explanation of a tautology must be. A short conclusion can require a much longer sequence of intermediate deductions. Restricting the depth of each intermediate formula limits the expressive power of individual statements while still allowing a long derivation and arbitrary reuse of earlier facts. Modular gates add compact statements about counts modulo p, such as parity when p=2. Krajíček gives the explicit modular axiom presentation used in this card.

The corresponding problem without modular gates has been solved. Ajtai’s work gives superpolynomial lower bounds for the pigeonhole principle in bounded-depth Frege, and Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo strengthen these to exponential bounds. Their argument uses restrictions adapted to the combinatorics of partial matchings. Permitting modular counting defeats the direct extension of that approach: a short parity statement can remain meaningful after many ordinary variables have been fixed.

Circuit complexity provides an analogy but not a solution. Razborov and Smolensky establish lower bounds for constant-depth Boolean circuits with prime modular gates. A proof, however, is a sequence of related formulas, and every tautology itself computes the constant true function. Showing that some nonconstant function requires a large circuit therefore does not directly force long proofs of tautologies. The February 2026 work of Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov explicitly identifies this remaining gap between circuit and proof lower bounds.

Resolution over parities is a much weaker subsystem whose lines are disjunctions of linear equations modulo two. Efremenko and Itsykson’s CCC 2025 work develops amortized closure and strengthens lifting lower bounds for restricted-depth parity-resolution refutations. The restriction there concerns the number of inference steps along a path in the derivation graph. That is different from the constant logical depth of each formula in AC⁰[p]-Frege. A long chain of shallow formulas remains allowed in the present question.

Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov’s February 2026 lifting theorem gives derivation depth Ω(w²/log S) for size-S parity-resolution proofs when the underlying CNF needs resolution width w. It also gives a pure quadratic size lower bound. These are meaningful advances, but a quadratic bound is polynomial, and a tradeoff requiring sufficiently deep proofs still permits polynomial-size proofs with large derivation depth. Neither gives the superpolynomial unrestricted proof-size target here.

Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret’s ITCS 2026 result studies explicit DNF formulas expressing the difficulty of proving certain algebraic circuit lower bounds. They show that these formulas do not all have polynomial-size AC⁰[p]-Frege proofs. The unresolved point is whether the formulas are tautologies: the theorem leaves open the possibility that some are simply false. They provide a conditional route to tautologicity through hardness of proving properties related to tensor rank. This separates two obligations that a completed lower-bound construction must satisfy.

Algebraic proof systems offer another route, but their representation restrictions matter. Hakoniemi, Limaye and Tzameret’s May 2026 work gives hard CNF instances for a fragment of the Ideal Proof System represented by read-once oblivious algebraic branching programs. It overcomes the obstacle that earlier lower bounds in that line concerned purely algebraic, non-Boolean instances. It does not remove the restricted representation of certificates or establish lower bounds for full modular Frege.

The quantifiers exclude a fixed-degree lower bound such as n¹⁰ and require failure of every polynomial size bound at every fixed line depth. They also keep the target formulas short and efficiently constructible, so hardness cannot come from writing an exponentially large conclusion or searching indefinitely for an unnamed formula. Resolving this frontier would extend lower-bound methods to formal reasoning that can perform modular counting, an ability missing from ordinary bounded-depth Frege.

cards.title: Superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted Frege proofs
cards.formal: Is the Frege proof system not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every C>0 and c≥1, does some propositional tautology φ have shortest Frege proof size s_F(φ)>C(|φ|+2)ᶜ?
cards.definitions: Use explicitly written Boolean formulas over propositional variables, negation ¬ and material implication →. Fix the axiom schemes A→(B→A), (A→(B→C))→((A→B)→(A→C)), and (¬B→¬A)→(A→B), where A,B,C may be replaced uniformly within an instance by any formulas. A proof is a finite sequence of formulas, each either an instance of one of these schemes or inferred from two earlier lines A and A→B by modus ponens. Its last line is φ. There are no undischarged assumptions and no extension rule introducing abbreviations for other formulas. Previously derived lines may be reused arbitrarily. Intermediate formulas may have arbitrary depth and length; there is no independent cap on a line’s size. Variables not occurring in φ may occur in ordinary axiom instances and inference lines. A tautology is a formula true under every Boolean assignment. Fix a standard binary encoding with variable indices in binary and explicitly encoded connectives, delimiters and inference references. The input size |φ| and the proof size are their full bit lengths, including every repeated formula occurrence. The minimum over all such proofs is s_F(φ). Standard finite Frege presentations are polynomially equivalent, so polynomial boundedness is independent of this choice of basis. The question concerns existence of proofs, without a uniform algorithm to generate either the hard tautologies or their shortest proofs.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that no one polynomial bounds the minimum Frege proof size of every tautology, or refute this by proving a universal bound s_F(φ)≤C(|φ|+2)ᶜ for fixed C,c. A fixed-degree lower bound, a lower bound for a restricted subsystem, or hardness of searching for proofs is not a complete affirmative answer. An explicit efficiently generated hard family would be a stronger form of a positive solution, but is not required by the quantified statement.
cards.why: A defining lower-bound problem for formal reasoning. It asks whether an elementary, robust and powerful language of efficiently checkable proofs necessarily fails to certify some short tautologies with polynomial-size derivations.

importance.reason: A central unresolved step in the Cook–Reckhow program, beyond the systems for which current general lower-bound methods succeed.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No unconditional superpolynomial lower bound for unrestricted Frege proof size was found in the checked primary sources. The April 2026 tree-like result has a line-size cap, the formalization result concerns bounded-depth proofs, and the June 2026 algebraic result does not translate into the required propositional lower bound.

context_blocks.text: Frege systems formalize ordinary propositional deduction with finitely many rule patterns. A proof may introduce a useful intermediate lemma, combine it with other lemmas and reuse it later. Each step is easy to check syntactically. The open question asks whether this familiar form of deduction must sometimes produce certificates whose size exceeds every polynomial in the statement being proved.

The distinction between the size of a statement and the number of its variables matters. A formula on n variables may itself have exponential length in n. An exponential lower bound expressed only in n can therefore be small relative to the actual input. This card compares the complete proof encoding directly with |φ|, and counts the sizes of all lines rather than treating a very large intermediate formula as a single unit of cost.

Cook and Reckhow placed these questions in a general theory of efficiently checkable proof systems. There exists some polynomially bounded propositional proof system if and only if NP=coNP. Consequently, NP≠coNP would imply a positive answer here. The reverse implication is not established: proving that this particular proof language is inefficient would leave open the possibility that a different language provides short certificates for every tautology.

Short certificates and efficient discovery are separate issues. A failed search through proofs of length at most a million says nothing about all longer proofs, and exponential running time for one search strategy does not establish a lower bound on the shortest proof. Even a universal polynomial size bound would be an existence theorem; it would not by itself supply a polynomial-time algorithm that finds those proofs.

The pigeonhole principle explains why lower bounds for weaker systems have not directly extended to Frege. Its propositional encoding asserts that n+1 pigeons cannot be injected into n holes. Although the familiar encoding requires exponentially large resolution refutations, Buss proved in 1987 that it has polynomial-size Frege proofs. The stronger system can organize counting arguments that clause-by-clause resolution cannot express economically.

Wigderson’s textbook records the unrestricted lower bound as Open Problem 6.10, after surveying systems that already admit strong lower bounds. Frege permits arbitrary Boolean formulas as intermediate assertions. Removing a fixed-depth restriction therefore changes the available reasoning, even if the final tautologies are shallow. A theorem about bounded-depth Frege must control all proofs allowed by its depth bound; it does not control proofs that use deeper intermediate lemmas.

A substantial 2026 result by de Rezende, Engström, Ghannane and Risse gives superpolynomial refutation-length lower bounds for tree-like Frege with bounded line size, including a stronger semantic version. Their explicit families contain formulas for which almost every sampled instance is hard under the prescribed cap. The result is useful because the restricted systems can still efficiently handle several standard combinatorial benchmarks.

The line cap is essential to interpreting that theorem. Without such a cap, ordinary tree-like Frege polynomially simulates general Frege. The usual simulation can enlarge intermediate formulas, however, so it does not preserve the restriction used by the new lower bound. In the semantic setting, sufficiently large lines can even package a whole inconsistent input at once. The paper explicitly explains this obstruction to transferring its theorem to unrestricted Frege.

Davis and Robere’s April 2026 work studies another layer: short proofs of statements asserting that certain bounded-depth proofs must be long. They show that a relatively weak system, Res(log), can formalize strong bounded-depth Frege lower bounds in the specified parameter regime. This is progress on the complexity of proving lower bounds themselves, while the underlying lower-bound target retains restrictions on depth and line size.

Alekseev’s June 2026 journal paper gives exponential bit-size lower bounds for a powerful algebraic system with extension variables. It emphasizes that its Binary Value Principle input is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size propositional CNF. Thus the algebraic theorem does not establish the propositional Frege lower bound, despite the strength of the algebraic proof system on suitable translations.

Extended Frege is a separate, stronger target elsewhere in the catalogue: it adds variables naming previously written computations. A lower bound for Extended Frege would imply one for Frege, whereas a Frege lower bound need not survive those abbreviations. The present question is already a central obstacle because it asks for a limitation on broad propositional reasoning with unrestricted intermediate formulas and unrestricted reuse of lemmas.

It concerns the shortest possible derivation, not the time spent by any particular proof-search strategy.
A lower bound would establish a substantial limitation on a familiar model of mathematical reasoning.
The saved review notes that powerful counting arguments give short Frege proofs where weaker systems struggle, and that separating Frege alone would not establish NP≠coNP.

cards.context:
Frege systems formalize ordinary propositional deduction with finitely many rule patterns. A proof may introduce a useful intermediate lemma, combine it with other lemmas and reuse it later. Each step is easy to check syntactically. The open question asks whether this familiar form of deduction must sometimes produce certificates whose size exceeds every polynomial in the statement being proved.

The distinction between the size of a statement and the number of its variables matters. A formula on n variables may itself have exponential length in n. An exponential lower bound expressed only in n can therefore be small relative to the actual input. This card compares the complete proof encoding directly with |φ|, and counts the sizes of all lines rather than treating a very large intermediate formula as a single unit of cost.

Cook and Reckhow placed these questions in a general theory of efficiently checkable proof systems. There exists some polynomially bounded propositional proof system if and only if NP=coNP. Consequently, NP≠coNP would imply a positive answer here. The reverse implication is not established: proving that this particular proof language is inefficient would leave open the possibility that a different language provides short certificates for every tautology.

Short certificates and efficient discovery are separate issues. A failed search through proofs of length at most a million says nothing about all longer proofs, and exponential running time for one search strategy does not establish a lower bound on the shortest proof. Even a universal polynomial size bound would be an existence theorem; it would not by itself supply a polynomial-time algorithm that finds those proofs.

The pigeonhole principle explains why lower bounds for weaker systems have not directly extended to Frege. Its propositional encoding asserts that n+1 pigeons cannot be injected into n holes. Although the familiar encoding requires exponentially large resolution refutations, Buss proved in 1987 that it has polynomial-size Frege proofs. The stronger system can organize counting arguments that clause-by-clause resolution cannot express economically.

Wigderson’s textbook records the unrestricted lower bound as Open Problem 6.10, after surveying systems that already admit strong lower bounds. Frege permits arbitrary Boolean formulas as intermediate assertions. Removing a fixed-depth restriction therefore changes the available reasoning, even if the final tautologies are shallow. A theorem about bounded-depth Frege must control all proofs allowed by its depth bound; it does not control proofs that use deeper intermediate lemmas.

A substantial 2026 result by de Rezende, Engström, Ghannane and Risse gives superpolynomial refutation-length lower bounds for tree-like Frege with bounded line size, including a stronger semantic version. Their explicit families contain formulas for which almost every sampled instance is hard under the prescribed cap. The result is useful because the restricted systems can still efficiently handle several standard combinatorial benchmarks.

The line cap is essential to interpreting that theorem. Without such a cap, ordinary tree-like Frege polynomially simulates general Frege. The usual simulation can enlarge intermediate formulas, however, so it does not preserve the restriction used by the new lower bound. In the semantic setting, sufficiently large lines can even package a whole inconsistent input at once. The paper explicitly explains this obstruction to transferring its theorem to unrestricted Frege.

Davis and Robere’s April 2026 work studies another layer: short proofs of statements asserting that certain bounded-depth proofs must be long. They show that a relatively weak system, Res(log), can formalize strong bounded-depth Frege lower bounds in the specified parameter regime. This is progress on the complexity of proving lower bounds themselves, while the underlying lower-bound target retains restrictions on depth and line size.

Alekseev’s June 2026 journal paper gives exponential bit-size lower bounds for a powerful algebraic system with extension variables. It emphasizes that its Binary Value Principle input is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size propositional CNF. Thus the algebraic theorem does not establish the propositional Frege lower bound, despite the strength of the algebraic proof system on suitable translations.

Extended Frege is a separate, stronger target elsewhere in the catalogue: it adds variables naming previously written computations. A lower bound for Extended Frege would imply one for Frege, whereas a Frege lower bound need not survive those abbreviations. The present question is already a central obstacle because it asks for a limitation on broad propositional reasoning with unrestricted intermediate formulas and unrestricted reuse of lemmas.

cards.definitions: Fix an explicit binary syntax for Boolean formulas built from indexed variables, AND, OR and NOT. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its variables; TAUT is the set of encodings of such formulas. A Cook–Reckhow proof system is a total function P:{0,1}*→TAUT, computed by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in its input length, whose range is all of TAUT. A string π proves formula F when P(π)=F. Soundness requires every output to be a tautology; completeness requires every tautology to occur as an output. There is no polynomial upper bound on the shortest proof of every formula. In this total-function presentation, strings that would be malformed proofs in a conventional calculus may instead produce a fixed tautology such as x₁∨¬x₁. A simulation translation is total and satisfies the equality on all strings, preserving the exact output formula. Its program, polynomial exponent and constants may depend on Q and P, but not on π. The order is ∃P ∀Q ∃t_Q ∀π. No algorithm taking an arbitrary program for Q and producing its translator is required. Neither advice, randomization nor an oracle is allowed in the systems or translations. Polynomial translation time also bounds the translated proof length polynomially in |π|.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one sound and complete polynomial-time proof system admits the required polynomial-time translations from every other such system, or prove that for every candidate P some sound and complete Q has no such translation. A proof-length comparison without an efficient translation proves only ordinary optimality. Refuting a particular named proof system’s p-optimality does not exclude all systems.

context_blocks.title: One common format for efficiently checked proofs
context_blocks.text: Different proof calculi can establish the same tautology with very different amounts of work. The question asks whether one format can accept a polynomial-time translation of any already-given proof in any other efficiently checkable format. The translator receives the proof; it is not being asked to discover a proof from the formula alone.

context_blocks.title: A simple simulation
context_blocks.text: Suppose Q is a proof system and another system merely adds a leading marker to each Q-proof. Removing the marker translates those proofs back with linear overhead. More generally, any fixed finite collection of sound systems can be combined using a system tag. The question quantifies over every sound polynomial-time system, so combining a predetermined finite list does not finish it.

context_blocks.title: Three distinct notions
context_blocks.text: Ordinary optimality asks only that comparably short proofs exist in the common system. P-optimality additionally asks for efficient translations of the given proofs. Polynomial boundedness instead asks that every tautology have a proof polynomial in the formula’s own length. A p-optimal system could still have very long proofs of some tautologies, so this target does not by itself say NP=coNP.

context_blocks.title: Known connections and current limits
context_blocks.text: Krajíček and Pudlák connect p-optimality with a tautology recognizer that is optimal up to polynomial overhead on positive inputs, compared with each other correct recognizer. Their theorem also gives the conditional implication from P=NP. Egidy’s February 2026 paper retains the question as open and proves limitations of relativizing arguments; the oracle supplied to those machines is extra computational power, absent from this card.

context_blocks.title: Later work on improving proof systems
context_blocks.text: The ICALP 2026 paper studies when the absence of an ordinary optimal system entails an effective procedure producing stronger systems. Its oracle and other-language results leave p-optimal propositional proof systems unresolved. Ordinary optimality, a procedure for improving systems, and efficient proof translation are related but separately quantified properties.

The translation must preserve the proved formula and run in time polynomial in the given proof length.

This is stronger than comparing proof lengths alone, and different from requiring short proofs of every tautology.
The 2026 oracle and jump-operator results leave the ordinary, oracle-free existence question open.

cards.title: A complete disjoint NP pair
cards.formal: Do disjoint languages A,B∈NP exist such that, for every disjoint pair C,D∈NP, there is a deterministic polynomial-time function f with f(C)⊆A and f(D)⊆B?
cards.definitions: All four languages consist of finite binary strings. NP means membership has a polynomial-length certificate checked by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. Disjoint means A∩B=∅ and C∩D=∅. The total function f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* may depend on (C,D); its running-time polynomial need not be universal across pairs. No requirement is imposed on f(x) when x∉C∪D. Completeness uses one function for both sides, not two unrelated reductions.

context_blocks.text: A disjoint NP pair expresses two efficiently certifiable cases that cannot occur together. Complete pairs would provide a universal object for this kind of promise complexity.

Canonical disjoint pairs arise from propositional proof systems, tying the question to proof simulation and finite incompleteness. The existence of a p-optimal proof system would imply a complete pair, but the converse is not asserted. This card asks the pair-completeness question itself.

cards.why: Test the existence of universal promise problems in a class closely connected with proof-system strength and feasible incompleteness.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

cards.title: Is k-Clique fixed-parameter tractable, equivalently FPT=W[1]?
cards.formal: Do there exist a total computable function f:ℕ→ℕ, a constant c, and one deterministic algorithm that decides whether an n-vertex graph contains a k-clique in time at most f(k)(n+2)ᶜ on every input? Equivalently, is FPT=W[1]?
cards.definitions: An instance is a finite simple undirected graph G on [n], encoded by its adjacency matrix, and an integer k with 0≤k≤n, encoded in binary. A k-clique is a set of k distinct vertices for which every pair is an edge; k=0 is a yes-instance. Inputs with k>n are rejected immediately, and other malformed inputs are rejected. The parameter is k, not treewidth, degree, or the size of a supplied decomposition. Running time counts deterministic Turing-machine steps on the full input. Constants and the function f may be arbitrary but must be fixed independently of n; the exponent c must also be independent of k. FPT comprises parameterized decision problems solvable in f(k)Nᶜ time, where N is their input encoding length. One equivalent definition of W[1] is the class of parameterized problems reducible to k-Clique by a deterministic f(k)Nᶜ-time many-one reduction whose output parameter is bounded by a computable function of k alone. This is the standard parameterized reduction convention under which Clique is W[1]-complete. No randomness, advice, or promise about G is allowed.

cards.status_note: Explicitly presented as the central open conjecture in Bottesch’s primary paper and the parameterized-algorithms textbook. Research through 10 September 2026 located no proof of equality or separation. Conditional lower bounds and improved fixed-k algorithms are recorded with their distinct quantifiers.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, 2^{2^k}n³ meets the requested form, while n^{k/10} does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If P=NP then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus FPT≠W[1] is a stronger separation conjecture than P≠NP in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every W[1] problem in FPT time. This is why a W[1]-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out f(k)n^{o(k)} algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is W[1]-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove FPT≠W[1].

cards.title: Does deterministic 3-SAT have a positive optimal exponential rate?
cards.formal: Is there a constant c>0 such that, for every deterministic algorithm A that correctly decides every 3-CNF satisfiability instance, and every constant d≥0, A does not have worst-case running time O(2^{cn}L^d)? Here n is the number of variables and L is the full binary input length. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH).
cards.definitions: A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of explicitly listed clauses, each containing at most three literals xᵢ or ¬xᵢ. Satisfiability means existence of a Boolean assignment satisfying all clauses. Variables are relabeled consecutively; n counts the distinct variables actually present, and L includes all literal indices, signs, delimiters, and repetitions. An empty clause is unsatisfiable and an empty conjunction is satisfiable. Algorithms are uniform deterministic Turing machines with no advice or oracles; they must halt and answer exactly on all inputs, with no promise about density, solution count, or distribution. Define s₃=inf{α≥0 : some such algorithm runs in O(2^{αn}L^d) for a fixed d}. ETH asserts s₃>0. The excluded exponent c is a single constant independent of the algorithm. The polynomial exponent and hidden constant may depend on the algorithm, but not the instance. Polynomial input factors allow the complete formula to be read even if clauses are repeated many times. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.

importance.reason: A foundational quantitative hardness hypothesis underlying exact, parameterized, graph, and geometric algorithm lower bounds.

Liu gives a deterministic 3-SAT upper bound with base 1.32793 using branching and generalized covering codes. The saving leaves a positive exponential rate.

cards.status_note: The cited foundational and 2026 conference sources treat ETH as an open hypothesis. Checked through 10 September 2026. This formulation is uniform, deterministic, and a positive-infimum assertion; randomized, nonuniform, gap, and stronger all-width hypotheses are distinct.

context_blocks.text: NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as 2^{√n} remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size n³, which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one 2^{o(n)} algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

There are substantial deterministic improvements over trying all 2ⁿ assignments. Liu combines branching with derandomized local search to obtain a 1.32793ⁿ bound for 3-SAT, up to polynomial factors. Such an algorithm decreases an upper bound on s₃ while leaving it positive. Empirical solver success, promises of many solutions, and bounded-occurrence restrictions do not address worst-case unrestricted formulas.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

cards.title: Can general weighted TSP be solved in O*((2−ε)^n) time?
cards.formal: Do there exist constants ε∈(0,1), c≥1 and a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every complete undirected graph on n≥3 labelled vertices with nonnegative binary-encoded integer edge weights of total encoding length L, outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle with probability at least 2/3 in worst-case time O((2−ε)^n(n+L)^c)?
cards.definitions: Each unordered pair of distinct vertices has one explicitly listed weight. A Hamiltonian cycle visits each vertex exactly once before returning to its first vertex, and its weight is the sum of its n edge weights. Output the cyclic list of vertex labels. The input has no metric, bounded-weight, planarity or sparsity promise. Use a random-access word RAM with w=B⌈n+log₂(L+2)⌉ bits per word for one fixed sufficiently large integer B; unit-cost operations are reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo 2^w and integer division by nonzero words. Integers occupying several words incur the cost of all word operations. This word size permits addressing exponential-space subset tables; its polynomial bit-operation overhead is already permitted by the polynomial factor in n+L. The running-time bound includes reading weights, preprocessing, random bits and output and holds on every execution. Only independent private fair random bits are allowed; there is no quantum access, advice or oracle. The constants ε,c,B and the implicit multiplicative constant are independent of n,L and the weights. A deterministic algorithm also qualifies. Dependence polynomial in the numerical maximum weight, rather than its binary length, does not qualify.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

context_blocks.text: The exact travelling salesman problem asks for a cheapest tour through all vertices. In the general weighted setting, discovering a Hamiltonian cycle is not enough: the input is complete, so tours certainly exist, but their costs can vary greatly. The computational target is the minimum among them.

The classical subset dynamic program has a base-two dependence on the number of vertices. Stoian’s 2024 algorithm improves the familiar O(2^n n²) time by a factor 2^{Ω(√log n)}. Its bound retains the exponential base two and does not yield O*((2−ε)^n) for any fixed positive ε.

This distinction is substantial even though both bounds are exponential. A fixed base reduction saves an exponential factor on increasingly large instances, whereas savings in the polynomial or subexponential prefactor do not. The card asks about unrestricted classical algorithms, not about the optimality of the original dynamic-programming recurrence.

Weight encoding separates this target from several related exact questions. A method whose time is polynomial in the maximum integer weight can be very expensive when a large weight has a short binary representation. Likewise, faster algorithms for unweighted Hamiltonicity or for special weighted graph classes do not establish the general weighted guarantee.

No asserted reduction from SETH is built into the question. The desired algorithmic existence is itself the target; a conditional lower bound must state its assumption separately. The Parameterized and exact algorithms bucket is appropriate because the defining issue is the exponential dependence on n, rather than polynomial-time approximation of a tour.

cards.title: Can twin-width be approximated in fixed-parameter time?
cards.formal: Do there exist total computable functions f,g:N→N and a constant c≥1, and one deterministic Turing machine A, such that for every finite nonempty simple graph G on n vertices and integer k≥0, A halts within f(k)(n+1)^c bit operations and either correctly reports tww(G)>k or outputs a contraction sequence of G of width at most g(k)? No order, decomposition or contraction sequence is supplied with G.
cards.definitions: The input gives n, the n×n adjacency matrix of G, and k in binary. A contraction sequence is a sequence of partitions of V(G), starting with the singleton partition and ending with {V(G)}, each obtained from its predecessor by merging two parts. For distinct parts X,Y, their pair is mixed if there exist both an adjacent pair x∈X,y∈Y and a nonadjacent pair x′∈X,y′∈Y in the original graph. The red degree of a part is the number of other parts with which it has a mixed pair. The sequence width is the maximum red degree over every part of every partition. Twin-width tww(G) is the minimum sequence width; a one-vertex graph has twin-width zero. The output lists the n−1 merges using integer part labels. Both f and g depend only on k, whereas c is independent of k and G. If tww(G)≤k, rejection is forbidden. If tww(G)>k, either a correct rejection or the stated bounded-width sequence is allowed.

cards.definitions: A k-expression is a finite expression building a labeled graph using labels from {1,…,k}. It can create one isolated vertex with a chosen label; take the disjoint union of two previously constructed labeled graphs; add all edges between the vertices labeled i and those labeled j for distinct i,j; or change every label i to j. Edge insertion leaves existing edges in place without duplicating them. Relabeling changes no edges. The two operands of a disjoint union may both be arbitrary expressions, so this is ordinary clique-width, not linear clique-width. For a nonempty graph G, cw(G) is the least k for which some k-expression produces a graph isomorphic to G after labels are erased. Set cw(∅)=0. The input contains n≥0 and the n×n symmetric zero-diagonal 0/1 adjacency matrix for the graph on {1,…,n}. It contains no construction expression or promise about its width. A_k outputs YES exactly when cw(G)≤k and NO otherwise, always halting with the stated worst-case bit bound. The quantifier order is ∀k ∃A_k,C_k,c_k ∀G: k is fixed for each machine, and the polynomial exponent may depend on it. Each A_k is a single finite program with no advice depending on graph size; the statement imposes no effective map from k to its program and no uniform exponent.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove polynomial-time exact recognition for every fixed threshold k in the model stated, or prove that for at least one fixed k the language {G:cw(G)≤k} has no deterministic polynomial-time decider. An expression with more than k labels does not establish a YES answer; failure of one construction does not establish NO. Variable-k NP-hardness, or fixed-k hardness under an unproved assumption, does not alone unconditionally refute this proposition.

context_blocks.title: A width that permits dense graphs
context_blocks.text: Clique-width counts reusable labels in a construction, not the size of a largest clique. Every nonempty edgeless graph has width 1. Complete graphs with at least two vertices have width 2, regardless of their size. Thus even very dense graphs can have small clique-width; the parameter captures how uniformly groups of vertices can be assembled.

context_blocks.title: Fixed thresholds versus the general optimization problem
context_blocks.text: Fellows and coauthors prove NP-completeness when both G and k are input. The present statement allows a different polynomial bound for each fixed k. For example, a hypothetical bound N^(k+2) would be polynomial for each such threshold, while not giving a polynomial bound when k grows with N. The source lists fixed-threshold recognition separately from the stronger FPT question, which asks for one algorithm with runtime f(k)N^c and c independent of k.

context_blocks.title: Small thresholds are understood
context_blocks.text: Polynomial-time recognition is known through k=3, with the full three-label algorithm published by Corneil and coauthors in 2012. The cited sources retain k=4 as the first unresolved threshold. A solution only for four labels would still leave the card’s quantification over every fixed k.

context_blocks.title: Approximate or supplied decompositions serve a different purpose
context_blocks.text: A procedure that returns an expression with f(k)>k labels for graphs of width at most k can enable other graph algorithms, yet leave the exact threshold undecided. Likewise, the July 2026 feedback-vertex-set result assumes a k-expression is already supplied. These results explain the usefulness of clique-width without providing the recognizer requested here.

cards.title: Can weighted independent set be solved in time polynomial in its optimal tropical circuit size?
cards.formal: Do there exist one deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,c≥1 such that for every finite simple graph G on n≥1 vertices and nonnegative integer weight vector w, A outputs the maximum independent-set weight within C(τ(G)+n+L+1)^c bit operations, where L is the total binary encoding length of w and τ(G) is the minimum size of a tropical MWIS circuit defined below? Only G and w are supplied; neither τ(G) nor a circuit is part of the input.
cards.definitions: G is given by its n×n adjacency matrix. The n nonnegative weights are binary integers with delimiters, all counted in L. A vertex set I is independent when no edge has both endpoints in I. MWIS(G,w)=max_{I independent}Σ_{v∈I}w_v, allowing I=∅ with weight zero. A tropical circuit for G is a finite acyclic circuit with one designated output, arbitrary fan-out, input gates labeled x_v or the constant 0, and binary internal gates labeled max or + with their ordinary real-number meanings. No other constants or operations are allowed. Size counts every gate, including input and constant gates. An MWIS circuit must output MWIS(G,x) for every vector x∈R_≥0^n, so its topology depends only on G. Define τ(G) as the minimum size of such a circuit. This minimum exists because finitely many independent sets can each be summed and their maximum computed. The output algorithm may use general deterministic computation, not only tropical operations. Constants C,c are uniform over all graphs and weight vectors.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. cards.title: Fixed-parameter tractability of graph isomorphism by rank-width
cards.formal: Do a computable function f:ℕ→ℕ, an absolute constant c and a deterministic algorithm exist which decide isomorphism of graphs G,H in time f(k)(|V(G)|+|V(H)|+2)^c, where k=max(rw(G),rw(H))?
cards.definitions: Graphs are finite simple undirected graphs given by adjacency matrices. Isomorphism is a vertex bijection preserving adjacency. For a graph G and X⊆V(G), the cut-rank is the rank over the two-element field of the adjacency submatrix with rows X and columns V(G)∖X. A rank decomposition is a tree of maximum degree three whose leaves are bijectively labeled by V(G). Every tree edge partitions the leaves and hence defines a cut-rank; the decomposition width is the maximum of those ranks. Rank-width rw(G) is the minimum width, with rw(G)=0 for at most one vertex. No decomposition or parameter value is supplied to the algorithm. The exponent c is independent of the rank-width.

context_blocks.text: Rank-width measures graph complexity through low-rank adjacency cuts and supports many structural algorithms. Graph isomorphism on bounded rank-width is tractable at each fixed width, but that does not by itself yield one exponent independent of the parameter.

Neuen’s 2026 survey identifies the remaining parameterized isomorphism frontiers. An n^{g(k)} algorithm or a quasipolynomial dependence involving n does not establish fixed-parameter tractability. The target concerns testing isomorphism, without additionally demanding canonization.

sentences: XNLP captures parameterized problems solvable nondeterministically with fixed-parameter polynomial time and space proportional to a parameter-dependent factor times log n.
The Slice-wise Polynomial Space Conjecture predicts a simultaneous time-space obstruction for every XNLP-hard problem.
It excludes algorithms taking n^(f(k)) time while using only f(k)n^c space, where c is an absolute constant.
Thus allowing a parameter-dependent polynomial time exponent is conjectured insufficient to obtain a fixed polynomial space exponent.
The conjecture would explain why familiar dynamic programs cannot always trade their large memory usage for slower but still slice-wise polynomial computation.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Densest k-Subgraph
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do there exist a universal constant C≥1 and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every finite simple undirected unweighted graph G=(V,E) and every integer 1≤k≤|V|, A(G,k) outputs a set S⊆V with |S|=k and |E(G[S])|≥OPT(G,k)/C, where OPT(G,k)=max_{T⊆V, |T|=k}|E(G[T])|?
cards.definitions: G is explicitly represented by its vertices and edges, and k is supplied in binary as part of the input. G[S] contains all edges of G with both endpoints in S; loops and parallel edges are absent. The running time is polynomial in the full input length with a fixed exponent independent of k. The same finite C must work for all graphs, all graph sizes and all choices of k; it cannot increase with n=|V| or with k. The output must be a vertex set, not only an estimate of the optimum. When OPT=0, every k-set meets the requirement. Because all feasible sets have the same cardinality, maximizing edge count, average degree 2|E(G[S])|/k, or edges per selected vertex gives the same approximation objective. No promise of a clique, graph expansion, metric edge weights or a random input distribution is supplied. This card fixes deterministic algorithms; a randomized constant-factor guarantee would be major progress but has a distinct derandomization requirement. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Densest k-Subgraph is a basic test of how well algorithms can identify a concentrated combinatorial structure. Its unresolved approximation landscape influences many reductions and separates strong evidence of difficulty from the hardness consequences currently obtainable from P≠NP.

importance.reason: A flagship approximation problem with a simple objective, a large algorithmic gap, strong conditional and relaxation barriers, and consequences for several other optimization problems.

progress.text: Bhaskara and coauthors obtain O(n^(1/4+ε)) approximation in polynomial time for each fixed ε; the exact quarter-power endpoint has quasipolynomial running time in this work.
Bhaskara and coauthors prove polynomial integrality gaps for strong SDP hierarchies, establishing barriers for those relaxations.
Manurangsi proves almost-polynomial-ratio hardness under ETH, with perfect completeness; the revised April 2017 manuscript appears at STOC 2017.
Chuzhoy and coauthors publish a 2-CSP conjecture and conditional superconstant NP-hardness for DkS, together with reductions to related graph objectives.
Liu, Liu, Ma and Konar publish an exact continuous penalization and a nonconvex optimization method; no general constant-factor polynomial-time guarantee is established.
Laekhanukit, Manurangsi and Trabelsi give reductions to Densest At-Least-k-Subgraph and explicitly retain the missing NP-hardness of even 1.001 approximation for DkS.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The constant-factor algorithm is already ruled out assuming ETH, which remains unproved. The May 2026 primary source explicitly notes the absence of NP-hardness of approximation even at factor 1.001. This card asks about a deterministic constant-factor algorithm on all unweighted graphs, and preserves the distinction between conditional evidence and an unconditional resolution.

context_blocks.text: The task asks for a fixed-size collection of vertices containing as many internal interactions as possible. The cardinality restriction is what turns an otherwise tractable density objective into a central approximation problem. Without a prescribed size, maximizing edges per vertex can be solved in polynomial time. Allowing at least k vertices also changes which solutions compete: a large moderately dense region may be a valid answer even when no comparably useful k-vertex portion can be extracted.

Exact optimization contains CLIQUE: a graph has a k-clique precisely when OPT(G,k)=k(k−1)/2. This observation alone gives almost no multiplicative approximation gap. A k-set missing only one possible edge is nearly optimal as k grows, even though it is not a clique. To rule out a constant-factor algorithm, a reduction must create a substantial separation between the best densities of its YES and NO instances, not merely a one-edge difference.

Bhaskara, Charikar, Chlamtac, Feige and Vijayaraghavan achieve O(n^(1/4+ε)) approximation in n^O(1/ε) time for every fixed ε>0. Their method uses small tree patterns and a hierarchy of conditioned information to identify a dense region. The O(n^(1/4)) phrase in the paper’s title needs care: attaining that endpoint in their analysis takes quasipolynomial n^O(log n) time. Neither rate is a constant approximation.

There is substantial evidence against the target. Manurangsi proves that ETH rules out even approximation within n^(1/(log log n)^a), for a universal constant a>0. ETH asserts that 3SAT has no 2^o(N)-time algorithm on N variables. This is a stronger assumption than P≠NP; the result therefore already excludes every fixed constant under ETH, while leaving the weaker-assumption hardness problem unresolved. Its YES instances can contain a k-clique, a property called perfect completeness.

Semidefinite-programming lower bounds supply a different kind of evidence. Bhaskara, Charikar, Guruswami, Vijayaraghavan and Zhou construct polynomial integrality gaps for strong hierarchies of relaxations. A relaxation can assign a large fractional or vector-valued objective even when no genuine k-set has comparable density. Such a gap limits approximation guarantees obtained from that relaxation, but it is not a theorem excluding every polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm.

Chuzhoy, Dalirrooyfard, Grinberg and Tan propose a 2-CSP hardness conjecture that would imply NP-hardness of approximating Densest k-Subgraph within 2^((log n)^ε) for some ε>0. Their paper also connects its approximability to graph partitioning, dense coloring and bounded-crossing subgraphs. Some connections use quasipolynomial reductions, so they should not be read as constant-factor polynomial-time equivalences. The conjectural premise remains a real part of the hardness claim.

Laekhanukit, Manurangsi and Trabelsi’s May 2026 paper still reports that no NP-hardness of approximation is known for Densest k-Subgraph even at factor 1.001. They show that the absence of any constant-factor DkS algorithm implies a (3/2−ε) barrier for the at-least-k density problem. This transfers a hypothetical negative answer to a neighboring objective; the neighboring problem’s known 2-approximation does not answer this card.

An AAAI 2026 result by Liu, Liu, Ma and Konar gives an exact continuous penalization reformulation and an efficient nonconvex proximal-gradient method. Exactness concerns the relationship between optima of the formulations. It does not mean the method finds a global optimum, or even a fixed approximation ratio, on every graph in polynomial time. The distinction explains how useful practical progress can coexist with the unresolved worst-case guarantee.

cards.title: Unique Games: is near-satisfiability NP-hard to distinguish from low value?
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every pair of rational constants ε,δ>0 with ε+δ<1, does there exist an integer q≥2 such that it is NP-hard to distinguish Unique Games instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon$ from instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta$? Here q is the alphabet size, fixed independently of the input graph, and val(G) is the largest fraction of constraints simultaneously satisfied by any labeling.
cards.definitions: An instance has finitely many vertices and a nonempty explicit list E of directed edges between distinct vertices; repeated edges are allowed and counted separately. Every vertex receives a label in [q]={1,…,q}. An edge e=(u,v) carries an explicitly given permutation π_e:[q]→[q] and is satisfied exactly when π_e(ℓ(u))=ℓ(v). Thus val(G)=max_ℓ |{e satisfied by ℓ}|/|E|. There are no graph expansion or degree promises. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT mapping every satisfiable formula into the ≥1−ε case and every unsatisfiable formula into the ≤δ case. The reduction, its running-time exponent, and q may depend on ε,δ. Inputs with value strictly between the thresholds are outside the promise. The question is the NP-hardness proposition itself; P≠NP is needed when drawing the usual conclusion that no polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm exists. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: UGC would turn many conditional approximation thresholds into NP-hardness theorems and explain the optimality of a general SDP framework. Its very simple permutation constraints isolate a fundamental boundary between exact consistency, approximate consistency, and hardness amplification.

importance.reason: An organizing conjecture for approximation thresholds, with consequences for whole families of constraint satisfaction problems and strong connections to SDP algorithms, PCPs, and analysis.

progress.text: Khot proposes the conjecture. Perfect satisfiability is polynomial-time decidable; the conjectured hard regime has positive completeness error and an alphabet depending on both gap parameters.

Raghavendra gives a general SDP and rounding framework for fixed finite-domain CSPs and transfers SDP integrality gaps to Unique-Games-based hardness. Under UGC, its achievable thresholds are optimal up to any fixed accuracy, unless P=NP.

Arora, Barak, and Steurer give, for an absolute α>0, an exp(q n^(ε^α))-time algorithm finding a (1−ε^α)-satisfying labeling in a (1−ε)-satisfiable q-label instance on n vertices. In the small fixed-ε regime this is subexponential, but not polynomial.

The line of work proving the 2-to-2 Games Theorem yields NP-hardness of Unique Games at completeness 1/2 and arbitrarily small soundness. Khot’s exposition states this explicitly as Theorem 2.20; it leaves the near-one completeness of UGC unresolved.

The journal version of Dinur, Khot, Kindler, Minzer, and Safra’s second installment documents its role in the proof sequence, while retaining the full Unique Games statement as Conjecture 1.4. Its publication is not a new proof of full UGC.

context_blocks.text: Each constraint is locally simple: fixing either endpoint label determines exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. Exact satisfiability of all constraints is decidable in polynomial time. Allowing a small fraction of constraints to fail changes the question sharply.

The conjecture says that an instance admitting an almost perfect assignment can nevertheless be hard to distinguish from one where every assignment fails almost everywhere. These are two promised regimes, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum. The alphabet is allowed to grow as the desired gap becomes more demanding. Indeed, a uniformly random labeling satisfies a 1/q fraction in expectation, so a soundness threshold below 1/q is impossible.

Raghavendra’s theorem connects such reductions to a general semidefinite-programming framework: under UGC, that framework achieves the approximation thresholds of fixed finite-domain constraint satisfaction problems, to arbitrary constant accuracy.

The strongest relevant hardness milestone must be read with its completeness parameter. The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies hardness for Unique Games with value at least one half versus arbitrarily small value. It does not make the yes instances almost perfectly satisfiable. Raising completeness from one half to arbitrarily close to one is precisely a remaining gap relevant to this card.

Algorithmic progress also matters even when it is slower than polynomial time. Subexponential algorithms exploit spectral decompositions of the constraint graph, limiting what quantitative hardness reductions could establish. Because a polynomial reduction can enlarge the instance by a parameter-dependent power, these algorithms coexist with the NP-hardness conjecture.

cards.title: A polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation for Directed Steiner Tree
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do there exist constants a≥1 and C≥1 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every feasible Directed Steiner Tree instance with k terminals, outputs a feasible subgraph of cost at most a(log₂(k+2))^C times optimum with probability at least 2/3?
cards.definitions: An instance consists of a finite directed graph G=(V,E), a root r∈V, a nonempty terminal set T⊆V∖{r} with k=|T|, and nonnegative rational arc costs c_e given exactly in binary. Every terminal is promised reachable from r; this can also be checked in polynomial time, with infeasibility reported otherwise. A feasible solution is an arc subset F⊆E such that (V,F) contains a directed path from r to every t∈T. Its cost is Σ_{e∈F}c_e, counting an arc once even if many paths use it. OPT is the minimum such cost. The algorithm must output a feasible subset on every execution and satisfy the approximation guarantee on every instance with probability at least 2/3 over its internal randomness. Its bit running time on every execution is bounded by one fixed polynomial in the entire input encoding length, including cost bits. The constants a,C and the polynomial are independent of n=|V|, k and the costs. If OPT=0, the successful output must also have zero cost. Local computation is ordinary uniform classical computation without advice or free optimization oracles. There is no planarity, acyclicity, bounded depth, bounded treewidth, metric, or supplied fractional-solution promise. The word tree refers to the optimization problem: any feasible subgraph may be returned, and redundant edges can be removed.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm and fixed constants satisfying these bounds, or prove that no such randomized polynomial-time algorithm exists. An O(k^ε)-approximation for every separately fixed ε>0, a polylogarithmic approximation taking quasipolynomial time, or a guarantee on a restricted graph class is partial progress. A gap for a particular LP relaxation limits that relaxation, not every algorithm. A hardness result ruling out only some smaller powers of log k does not exclude all fixed powers and therefore does not refute this proposition.
cards.why: A defining gap in directed network-design approximation: determine whether a shared directed connection network can be approximated within a polylogarithmic factor using only polynomial time.

importance.reason: A central approximation problem encompassing covering and rooted network design, with a persistent gap between polynomial and quasipolynomial algorithms.

progress.text: Classical directed Steiner approximation algorithms give O(k^ε) for every fixed ε>0 in polynomial time.
Grandoni–Laekhanukit–Li obtain O(log² k/log log k) in quasipolynomial time, with conditional matching-scale hardness.
Friggstad–Mousavi obtain a polynomial-time O(log k)-approximation for planar digraphs.
Chekuri and coauthors extend planar rooted-network techniques and prove an O(log² k) planar LP gap.
Version 2 of Laekhanukit’s initial general claim is withdrawn.
Version 3 narrows that claim to access to a relatively integral fractional solution; the record retains its withdrawal comment.
Chekuri–Jain obtain planar length-constrained bicriteria approximations and explicitly retain the general polynomial-time polylogarithmic question.
