cards.status_note: The July 2026 primary literature explicitly leaves this general-graph question open. The inherited 2024 claim was withdrawn, and its October 2025 replacement is restricted to a special supplied fractional solution; that claim is not counted as an established general result. Planar and quasipolynomial algorithms do not satisfy this card. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: The problem asks how cheaply a root can reach many destinations through one shared directed network. Buying a common initial segment can save cost across many root-to-terminal paths, but the directions restrict which branching structures are usable. With one terminal the problem is shortest path. With many terminals, selecting where the paths should share infrastructure becomes the central optimization challenge.

A simple reduction explains why ordinary reachability is insufficient. For a set-cover instance, create a vertex for each set and each element, an arc of cost one from the root to every set vertex, and zero-cost arcs from each set to its elements. Make all element vertices terminals. A feasible network must buy a collection of set arcs covering all elements, and its cost equals the number of chosen sets. The directed graph can thus encode a nontrivial covering problem even with only two layers after the root.

The familiar polynomial-time approximation frontier is O(k^ε) for every fixed ε>0, from the classical directed Steiner algorithms. The running-time exponent depends on the chosen accuracy parameter. Setting ε to a quantity that shrinks with k is not a free improvement: it changes that dependence and can produce quasipolynomial time. A power of k, however small and fixed, eventually exceeds every fixed power of log k.

Grandoni, Laekhanukit and Li obtain an O(log² k/log log k)-approximation in quasipolynomial time. Their techniques combine a structured reduction with a hierarchy of strengthened linear relaxations and dependent rounding. This establishes that a good approximation exists at a slower time scale. The requested advance is to achieve some polylogarithmic factor with a fixed polynomial running-time exponent; matching the sharper quasipolynomial factor is not required.

The same work gives near-matching quasipolynomial-time hardness under additional complexity assumptions, including the Projection Games Conjecture. This does not show that every polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation is impossible: a larger fixed logarithmic power is allowed in this card. The issue is a gap between what can currently be computed in polynomial time and what is known with more time, rather than the already settled hardness of exact optimization.

A natural flow relaxation buys a fractional capacity x_e for each arc and, separately for each terminal, sends a unit flow from the root using at most x_e on that arc. Different terminals may reuse the same purchased capacity because a network edge is bought once. In general graphs this relaxation has polynomial-size integrality gaps, including Ω(√k) examples. Those examples explain why a straightforward LP-rounding strategy cannot guarantee a polylogarithmic factor against that relaxation on every instance. They do not rule out stronger relaxations or a different algorithm.

The inherited Laekhanukit reference requires careful version tracking. Its December 2024 general claim was withdrawn in version 2. Version 3, submitted in October 2025, presents itself as a rectification restricted to a relatively integral fractional solution: each terminal flow on an edge is either zero or the entire purchased capacity. The record still displays the earlier withdrawal comment about a reachability-proof error. This card treats the later restricted statement as a reported claim, not an established general approximation; finding an appropriate fractional solution is an additional requirement.

Planarity changes the picture substantially. Friggstad and Mousavi give a polynomial-time O(log k)-approximation for planar directed graphs, using shortest-path separators. Later work extends the structural approach to other rooted planar network-design problems and bounds a natural planar LP gap by O(log² k). These theorems show that directedness alone does not preclude the requested factor, but their separator arguments do not apply to arbitrary directed graphs.

Chekuri and Jain’s July 2026 work extends planar results to length-constrained network design. Its guarantees are bicriteria: they approximate cost while allowing an O(log k) multiplicative violation of the path-length constraint. The paper explicitly retains the general Directed Steiner Tree approximation question as open. Removing a length constraint or changing the objective does not remove the planarity hypothesis needed by those algorithms.

The requested advance is to achieve some polylogarithmic factor with a fixed polynomial running-time exponent; matching the sharper quasipolynomial factor is not required.

The same work gives near-matching quasipolynomial-time hardness under additional complexity assumptions, including the Projection Games Conjecture. This does not show that every polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation is impossible: a larger fixed logarithmic power is allowed in this card. The issue is a gap between what can currently be computed in polynomial time and what is known with more time, rather than the already settled hardness of exact optimization.

A natural flow relaxation buys a fractional capacity x_e for each arc and, separately for each terminal, sends a unit flow from the root using at most x_e on that arc. Different terminals may reuse the same purchased capacity because a network edge is bought once. In general graphs this relaxation has polynomial-size integrality gaps, including Ω(√k) examples. Those examples explain why a straightforward LP-rounding strategy cannot guarantee a polylogarithmic factor against that relaxation on every instance. They do not rule out stronger relaxations or a different algorithm.

The inherited Laekhanukit reference requires careful version tracking. Its December 2024 general claim was withdrawn in version 2. Version 3, submitted in October 2025, presents itself as a rectification restricted to a relatively integral fractional solution: each terminal flow on an edge is either zero or the entire purchased capacity. The record still displays the earlier withdrawal comment about a reachability-proof error. This card treats the later restricted statement as a reported claim, not an established general approximation; finding an appropriate fractional solution is an additional requirement.

Planarity changes the picture substantially. Friggstad and Mousavi give a polynomial-time O(log k)-approximation for planar directed graphs, using shortest-path separators. Later work extends the structural approach to other rooted planar network-design problems and bounds a natural planar LP gap by O(log² k). These theorems show that directedness alone does not preclude the requested factor, but their separator arguments do not apply to arbitrary directed graphs.

Chekuri and Jain’s July 2026 work extends planar results to length-constrained network design. Its guarantees are bicriteria: they approximate cost while allowing an O(log k) multiplicative violation of the path-length constraint. The paper explicitly retains the general Directed Steiner Tree approximation question as open. Removing a length constraint or changing the objective does not remove the planarity hypothesis needed by those algorithms.

cards.title: The Small-Set Expansion Hypothesis
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every rational constant η∈(0,1/2), is there a rational constant δ∈(0,1/2) such that the following promise problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a regular graph G on n vertices with δn an integer, distinguish YES: some S⊆V(G) with |S|=δn has Φ_G(S)≤η, from NO: every S⊆V(G) with |S|=δn has Φ_G(S)≥1−η.

cards.definitions: Use finite simple undirected d-regular graphs G=([n],E), n≥2 and d≥1, given explicitly by their adjacency matrices. Regular means that every vertex has exactly d neighbours; d is not a fixed constant or an extra promise. For nonempty S, ∂_G S is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and Φ_G(S)=|∂_G S|/(d|S|). Internal edges contribute twice to d|S| and zero to the boundary. This is normalized edge expansion, not the number of outside neighbours. The graph has no promised connectivity, geometry or spectral gap. The constants η,δ are chosen before the input; they are not parameters tending to zero with n. For δ=a/b in lowest terms, inputs have n a positive multiple of b, so exact set size has no rounding ambiguity. The YES and NO cases are disjoint since η<1/2; inputs meeting neither case have no required decision answer. NP-hardness means that for every language L with polynomially checkable witnesses, a deterministic polynomial-time map sends each x∈L to a YES graph and each x∉L to a NO graph. Equivalently, it suffices to supply such a reduction from Boolean satisfiability. Reduction constants and the polynomial exponent may depend on η and its chosen δ. The card fixes the unweighted regular-graph, exact-cardinality version of the imported question; weighted-volume, randomized-hardness and size-interval versions must be identified when cited.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves the stated NP-hardness for every η by choosing δ and giving a valid promise-preserving reduction. A negative resolution refutes this quantified hardness statement for some fixed η. Polynomial-time algorithms for every fixed δ at that η would refute the hardness claim under P≠NP; an algorithm alone must not be called an unconditional disproof of NP-hardness. Results restricted to special graph classes or allowing a different output set size do not automatically settle this formulation.

context_blocks.title: What expansion measures
context_blocks.text: Choose a vertex uniformly from S, then choose one of its neighbours uniformly. The probability of leaving S is exactly Φ_G(S). A set with expansion near zero is a group whose connections mostly remain inside it. Expansion near one means that almost every connection goes out. The promise asks whether one unusually insulated set exists at the specified size, or whether every set of that size is almost completely exposed.

context_blocks.title: Small means a fixed fraction
context_blocks.text: If δ=1/1000, the target has one thousand vertices in a million-vertex graph and one million vertices in a billion-vertex graph. Its size still grows linearly with n. Enumerating all sets of a fixed number of vertices therefore does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for the question. The order of constants also matters: δ may depend on the desired expansion gap η, and an algorithm for one convenient pair of constants would not refute the full hypothesis.

context_blocks.title: A sparse large cut can miss the issue
context_blocks.text: Take the disjoint union of two complete graphs on 50 vertices. Either whole component has expansion zero. Yet a two-vertex set contained in one component has expansion 48/49, and a two-vertex set split between the components has expansion one. Thus every set of the specified small size expands very well even though a larger zero-expansion cut exists. Optimizing over all sets up to half the graph can answer a different question from the exact small-size promise.

context_blocks.title: Why a large gap remains difficult
context_blocks.text: For a proposed set, its size and edge boundary are easy to count. The universal NO condition ranges over all sets of that size. The hypothesis asserts hardness even though YES and NO graphs are separated by a wide gap, with many intermediate graphs excluded by the promise. A graph expansion construction, a bound on one spectral parameter, or an algorithm with an uncontrolled change in set size is not automatically a distinguisher for this promise.

context_blocks.title: Connections and current boundary
context_blocks.text: Raghavendra and Steurer reduce small-set expansion to Unique Games, making this hypothesis a sufficient foundation for Unique Games hardness. Raghavendra, Steurer and Tulsiani relate it to a version of Unique Games with an additional expansion requirement and derive conditional hardness for graph partitioning and arrangement problems. This does not establish equivalence to unrestricted Unique Games in both directions. In August 2026, Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff use a randomized, weighted, exact-volume variant to prove a sparse least-squares hardness result. Such an application assumes an SSE statement; it does not prove the statement itself, and its modeling conventions should not be silently transferred to this card. The checked sources leave the hypothesis unresolved.

sentences: Is it NP-hard to distinguish one poorly expanding small set from uniformly strong expansion at the same set size?
The target set occupies a fixed fraction δ of the graph, with δ chosen after the gap parameter η.
Expansion is the fraction of incident edges that leave the set.
A sparse cut of a larger size does not necessarily reveal any poorly expanding set of the target size.
Known reductions connect the hypothesis to Unique Games and conditional hardness without resolving it.

cards.title: The 4/3 conjecture for the metric TSP subtour relaxation
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Let Γ=sup_{n≥3,c} OPT_TSP(c)/OPT_LP(c), where c ranges over all metrics on n labeled points and OPT_LP is the subtour relaxation defined below. Is Γ=4/3?
cards.definitions: For V={1,…,n} and E={{u,v}:u≠v}, a metric has c_uu=0, c_uv=c_vu>0 for u≠v, and c_uv≤c_uw+c_wv. Costs are arbitrary real numbers; no Euclidean embedding is assumed. OPT_TSP is the minimum sum of edge costs on a Hamiltonian cycle of the complete undirected graph. For S⊆V, δ(S) contains edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and x(F)=Σ_{e∈F}x_e. Define OPT_LP=min Σ_e c_e x_e subject to x(δ({v}))=2 for every v, x(δ(S))≥2 for every nonempty proper S⊊V, and 0≤x_e≤1 for every e. The LP is feasible and has positive optimum. The supremum ranges over every finite size, not one fixed n. This is the symmetric metric subtour-LP integrality gap, not an approximation ratio measured only against OPT_TSP, an asymmetric TSP relaxation, or a restricted geometric metric.
cards.answer_criterion: Known constructions establish Γ≥4/3. Thus an affirmative resolution proves OPT_TSP(c)≤(4/3)OPT_LP(c) for every finite metric instance. A negative resolution gives an instance with ratio strictly greater than 4/3, or proves such an instance exists. A supremum need not be attained to make the question meaningful. Improving an algorithm’s upper bound while it remains above 4/3 is progress, not a resolution.
cards.why: The exact strength of the principal relaxation for a canonical optimization problem, joining polyhedral structure, probabilistic rounding and approximation. A resolution would explain a longstanding gap between fractional connectivity and integral tours.

importance.reason: A defining integrality-gap conjecture in combinatorial optimization with consequences for LP rounding and the limits of metric TSP approximation methods.

Jin–Klein–Williamson’s journal article proves 4/3 for the half-integral cycle-cut class; its preprint first appeared in 2022.

cards.status_note: The general 4/3 equality remains open through the primary-source review of 11 September 2026. The established explicit upper bound recorded here is 3/2−2.18·10^{−34}; a September 2 preprint claims a further small improvement, clearly separated from verified literature. Restricted-class theorems and finite-size verification do not resolve the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.text: The relaxation allows fractional edge purchases while retaining two elementary properties of every tour: each vertex has degree two, and every nontrivial cut is crossed at least twice. It therefore knows much more than a disconnected cycle-cover relaxation, but its feasible points need not be convex combinations of Hamiltonian cycles. The conjecture asks for the exact worst loss caused by that remaining freedom.

For example, a feasible fractional vector may put positive weight on several alternative connections at one vertex without choosing a single predecessor and successor. The cut inequalities ensure aggregate connectivity, yet they do not force these local choices to assemble into one integral cycle. The proposed factor 4/3 says that, in a metric, repairing all such inconsistencies never costs more than one third of the fractional optimum.

The metric assumption is what makes shortcutting possible. If a connected Eulerian multigraph visits a vertex several times, replacing a detour by the direct edge between its endpoints does not increase cost. One can consequently search for a suitably cheap Eulerian structure rather than construct a Hamiltonian cycle at every intermediate step. This observation explains why spanning trees and parity correction recur in approximation algorithms for the problem.

A minimum spanning tree followed by a minimum-cost matching on its odd-degree vertices yields the classical 3/2 guarantee. Wolsey’s analysis measures both components against the LP: the tree costs at most the fractional optimum, and the matching at most half that value. The inherited July 2026 paper recalls this argument before studying a particular randomized refinement.

An algorithmic ratio and an integrality-gap ratio must use the correct denominator. A guarantee cost≤α·OPT_TSP does not establish OPT_TSP≤α·OPT_LP, since the fractional optimum can be smaller. Karlin–Klein–Oveis Gharan’s FOCS 2022 result explicitly supplies an LP-relative guarantee below 3/2, extending the earlier approximation breakthrough. It is this later theorem that directly improves the general gap bound.

The modern approach samples a spanning tree from a distribution constrained by fractional edge marginals, then corrects its parity. Tree cost and parity-repair cost interact, so treating the two separately can lose the desired saving. Gurvits–Klein–Leake strengthen probability estimates using capacities of real stable polynomials. Their Lemma 4.5 is explicitly LP-relative and yields the certified bound Γ≤3/2−2.18·10^{−34}. The small constant reflects a worst-case proof, not a claim that practical tours are that close to 3/2.

A class can have a better integrality gap than the worst ratio of a particular algorithm on it. Jin–Klein–Williamson prove the 4/3 bound for half-integral cycle-cut instances using a specialized construction. Half-integral means that nonzero fractional coordinates are 1/2 or 1, with an additional restriction on the hierarchy of tight cuts. This result does not cover every half-integral instance, still less every subtour solution.

Their July 2026 paper, which supplied the inherited reference, proves a 10/7 guarantee for the maximum-entropy algorithm on that same restricted class. Since 10/7 exceeds 4/3, it improves understanding of the chosen algorithm rather than improving the already-known class gap. The authors also identify examples giving a lower bound of 11/8 on the algorithm’s performance. Such an algorithm-specific obstruction cannot refute the conjecture about the cheapest possible tour.

Two complementary approaches restrict the fractional solution in other ways. Villa–Vercesi–Barta–Mastrolilli prove the 4/3 bound when an optimal solution has at most n+6 nonzero components, combining structural reasoning and computation. This is a support-size condition, not a theorem for every instance on at most n+6 vertices. Larger support remains outside its stated guarantee.

Cook–Hougardy–Petrich’s September 8, 2026 revision reports exact verification for all metric instances through n=16 and for half-integral extreme points through n=18. It also repairs omissions in earlier extreme-point lists. This is stronger evidence than sampling finitely many random metrics, because the computation organizes the relevant polyhedral cases. It still leaves unbounded n, and the catalogue has not rerun that enumeration.

A September 2 preprint by Zhao Song claims a larger universal saving, ε★>2.05522·10^{−30}, through a refined maximum-entropy analysis. Its main theorem is explicitly relative to OPT_LP. The statement was checked, but the lengthy proof and numerical certificate were not independently verified here, so the value is recorded as a recent claim rather than silently replacing the established bound. Even if confirmed, it would remain far above the requested ratio 4/3.

cards.title: Can metric k-Median reach the 1+2/e threshold?
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), does a randomized polynomial-time (1+2/e+ε)-approximation algorithm exist for general metric k-Median that always opens at most k facilities?
cards.definitions: An input consists of a finite set V, a full table of nonnegative rational distances d on V encoded in binary, nonempty subsets C,F⊆V of clients and allowable facilities with C∪F=V, and an integer 1≤k≤|F|. The table is promised to satisfy d(u,v)=d(v,u), d(u,v)=0 exactly when u=v, and the triangle inequality. Each client has unit demand. For nonempty S⊆F define cost(S)=Σ_{c∈C}min_{s∈S}d(c,s), and OPT=min{cost(S):S⊆F,1≤|S|≤k}. L is the total bit length of the input. For each fixed ε the target is one uniform classical randomized algorithm A_ε, with constants K_ε,d_ε such that every execution takes at most K_ε L^{d_ε} bit operations. It always returns an explicit nonempty S⊆F with |S|≤k, and on each input Pr[cost(S)≤(1+2/e+ε)OPT]≥2/3. Here e is the base of the natural logarithm. The constants may depend on ε but not on k, |C|, |F| or distance precision. No Euclidean, low-dimensional, stability, capacity or input-distribution promise is made. Candidate facilities are part of the input and cannot be enlarged. The guarantee also covers OPT=0.
cards.answer_criterion: Give the stated algorithms for every fixed ε>0, or rule them out for at least one fixed ε, explicitly identifying any complexity assumption used. This card fixes the yes/no question of approaching the known hardness threshold; it does not additionally require finding a different exact threshold after a negative answer. An algorithm opening k facilities only in expectation, one allowing k+o(k) facilities, or an FPT algorithm with unrestricted dependence on k does not prove the claim.
cards.why: A central unresolved approximation threshold for metric clustering, separating known coverage hardness from the best algorithms with a strict facility budget.

importance.reason: A major optimization problem with a substantial remaining algorithm–hardness gap and connections to coverage, facility location, LP rounding and parameterized approximation.

progress.text: Feige proves the 1−1/e hardness threshold for Max k-Cover, which yields the 1+2/e metric k-Median gap through a client–facility metric construction.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The checked general-metric result remains 2+ε with a strict budget, while the classical hardness threshold is 1+2/e. The FPT algorithm, Euclidean schemes and 2026 k-Means results do not settle the polynomial-time target here.

context_blocks.text: Metric k-Median selects a limited number of service locations and minimizes total distance to the nearest selected location. The number of clients and the number of candidate facilities may differ, and the distance table need not come from a Euclidean embedding. The same formulation models representative selection for clustering and placement of facilities. Its simplicity makes the unresolved approximation threshold a central benchmark for algorithm design.

The two endpoint numbers are approximately 1.73576 and 2. The lower endpoint is the classical hardness threshold 1+2/e; the best general feasible guarantee in the checked literature is 2+ε. The inherited STOC 2025 paper explicitly asks for a tight approximation result after obtaining that upper bound. Asking for 1+2/e+ε for every fixed ε avoids requiring that an infimum approximation ratio be achieved exactly.

The coverage origin of the lower endpoint can be seen directly. Represent each set as a candidate facility and each universe element as a client. Give a client–facility pair distance one when the set contains the element and distance three otherwise, and give distinct pairs on the same side distance two. These distances satisfy the triangle inequality. A collection of k sets covering a fraction p of the elements then has clustering cost (3−2p) times the universe size.

Feige’s Max k-Cover gap distinguishes complete coverage from coverage of at most 1−1/e+η, for any fixed η>0. Under the preceding metric construction this becomes a gap between cost one per client and cost at least 1+2/e−2η per client. This is why the constant is not an arbitrary numerical target. A randomized algorithm beating that gap on every input would yield randomized algorithms for the underlying NP-hard decision problem; the appropriate exclusion is NP≠RP for this card’s success convention.

Jain–Mahdian–Saberi’s 2002 paper gives the classical metric k-Median lower bound through a reduction to approximating Set Cover. Its historical statement uses the then-known slightly-superpolynomial-time assumption for Set Cover hardness. The coverage reduction above explains the stronger ordinary NP-hardness formulation without silently changing the assumption in the original theorem. Neither lower-bound route excludes approximation from just above 1+2/e.

The 2025 algorithm combines two components. One permits a logarithmic number of extra centers while retaining a 2+ε cost bound; another handles instances where deleting one optimal center increases the optimum substantially. Combining them returns a feasible solution opening at most k centers. The full paper’s May 2026 revision retains this result. It is therefore incorrect to describe the headline 2+ε theorem as only a bicriteria approximation.

The usual linear relaxation has a separate barrier near two. It uses fractional openings y_s, assignments x_{c,s}≤y_s, unit total assignment for each client, and Σ_s y_s≤k. For a star with q≥3 leaves, all vertices available as facilities, clients at the leaves and k=q−1, every integral optimum has cost two. Set the central opening to 1/(q−1), each leaf opening to (q−2)/(q−1), and assign each client’s remaining fraction to the center. This feasible LP solution costs q/(q−1), giving an integrality gap approaching two.

That explicit example limits a guarantee measured against this relaxation, not every polynomial algorithm measured against OPT. A sharper algorithm might use additional constraints, a different relaxation, or another method. Likewise, a lower bound for one rounding framework is not a computational impossibility theorem for the original optimization problem. The card’s target is deliberately stated using the true integral optimum.

There is already a matching-threshold algorithm in a different runtime regime. Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li’s ICALP 2019 work achieves 1+2/e+ε in fixed-parameter time with respect to k. The potentially large dependence on the number of opened facilities is permitted there. This does not supply a polynomial-time algorithm when k grows as part of the input, but it shows that the target ratio has meaningful algorithmic support.

A 2026 development concerns geometric input. Cohen-Addad and coauthors improve approximation-scheme runtimes in low-dimensional Euclidean spaces, where additional structure is available. Such a scheme does not apply to arbitrary distance tables.

Anand and coauthors’ July 2026 spectral dual-fitting paper improves k-Means guarantees, including in general metrics. That objective sums squared distances; squaring changes both the analysis and the hardness constants. It does not establish the stated k-Median ratio.

Resolving this question would determine whether the coverage obstruction captures the full cost of efficient metric clustering. A positive answer would bridge the remaining gap beyond the familiar LP benchmark. A stronger hardness threshold would reveal an obstruction not expressed by coverage alone. The exact facility budget is essential to either conclusion: averaging an excessive number of facilities over random choices changes the feasible problem.

cards.title: A constant improvement over factor two for Vertex Cover
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do a constant ε∈(0,1) and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm exist which, on every finite simple undirected graph G, output a vertex cover of size at most (2−ε)τ(G)?
cards.definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. A vertex cover is a subset S of the vertices containing at least one endpoint of every edge; τ(G) is the minimum size of such a set. The graph is represented by its adjacency matrix. The same ε and algorithm must work for graphs of all sizes, with no promise on degree, coloring or graph class. An edgeless input requires the empty cover. The question asks for an unconditional algorithm or unconditional refutation of its existence.

context_blocks.text: Vertex Cover is one of the canonical NP-hard covering problems and has a simple factor-two approximation. The absence of a fixed improvement despite extensive work makes the factor a central approximation barrier.

Unique Games implies hardness below two, while unconditional NP-hardness leaves a gap. A restricted graph-class algorithm does not answer the universal target. The source seminar situates the question in the development of approximation algorithms and primal-dual methods.

references.title: Research reference · epubs.siam.org

cards.definitions: A directed metric is a function c:V×V→R≥0 with c(i,i)=0 and c(i,k)≤c(i,j)+c(j,k) for all i,j,k. Symmetry is not required, and distinct vertices may have zero distance. The complete directed graph has one arc (i,j) for each i≠j and no loops. A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once before returning to its start; its cost is the sum of its n arc costs. OPT_ATSP(c) is the minimum over all such cycles. For S⊆V, δ⁺(S)={(i,j):i∈S,j∉S} and δ⁻(S)={(i,j):i∉S,j∈S}; for a set of arcs F write x(F)=Σ_(i,j)∈F x_ij. LP_ATSP(c) minimizes Σ_i≠j c(i,j)x_ij over real variables x_ij≥0 subject to x(δ⁺({v}))=x(δ⁻({v}))=1 for every v, and x(δ⁺(S))≥1 for every nonempty proper S⊊V. The degree equalities imply x(δ⁺(S))=x(δ⁻(S)), so an additional incoming-cut inequality would be redundant. No integrality restriction is placed on x. The feasible set is nonempty and compact; both optima are attained. The inequality, rather than division by LP_ATSP(c), also covers zero-cost instances. For positive LP value, the integrality ratio is OPT_ATSP(c)/LP_ATSP(c), and the overall gap is its supremum over all n and directed metrics. The question is a universal comparison of optimum values, without a running-time restriction on finding the tour. It concerns closed tours, not a prescribed-start/end path.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed factor-2 inequality for every finite directed metric and every size, or exhibit a finite directed metric with a rigorously proved strict violation. An affirmative answer need not attain ratio 2 on a finite instance: known families approach 2. An approximation algorithm proved only relative to the true tour optimum, or a result restricted to a subset of LP extreme points, does not establish the universal LP inequality.

context_blocks.title: Buying fractions of directed arcs
context_blocks.text: A tour buys each used arc completely. The relaxation permits fractional amounts of several arcs, while requiring one unit to enter and leave every city and at least one unit to leave every proper group of cities. Every tour is feasible for the LP, so the LP gives a lower bound on the tour cost. The question asks whether converting the best fractional cost into an actual tour ever entails a factor larger than two. A fractional solution need not be a probability distribution over whole tours.

context_blocks.title: Why subtour constraints matter
context_blocks.text: Suppose six cities form two groups of three, with travel cost 1 within a group and 10 between groups. Two separate three-city directed cycles satisfy every degree condition and cost only 6, but do not form a tour visiting all cities. The cut inequality for either group rules out this disconnected solution. These inequalities therefore add a global requirement to the local degree constraints; whether that requirement is strong enough to keep the full gap at two is the unresolved issue.

context_blocks.title: The current general gap
context_blocks.text: Families of directed instances have ratios tending to 2, so no smaller universal factor can work. Traub and Vygen’s 2022 article establishes an upper bound of 22. Their 2024 book improves the proved bound to 17 and explicitly retains the factor-2 question. Its circulation LP has the same optimum as the degree-constrained LP on directed metrics, so the model matches this card. The book also notes room for a small further numerical improvement; 17 is a stated theorem, not a claim that no refinement exists.

context_blocks.title: Finite computations and half-integral vertices
context_blocks.text: Vercesi and coauthors construct improved lower-bound instances at particular sizes. The June 2026 revision by Sosso, Bernardelli and Gualandi computes the gaps for all half-integral extreme points through twelve vertices, where half-integral means coordinates in {0,1/2,1}. An extreme point is a feasible LP solution that cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct feasible solutions. Other denominators and arbitrarily large instances remain outside that enumeration. These computations add evidence without proving the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.title: What a resolution would establish
context_blocks.text: The comparison measures the strength of this specific relaxation. A polynomial-time method achieving cost at most twice the LP optimum would settle the inequality and give an approximation guarantee, but the existence inequality itself does not promise an efficient construction. The symmetric metric TSP has a different classical 4/3 conjecture; its constants and finite verifications do not transfer to the larger family in which travel costs can depend on direction.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for uniform Sparsest Cut
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do a universal C≥1 and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist which, on every finite simple undirected graph G on n≥2 vertices, output a nonempty proper set S with φ_G(S)≤C min_{∅≠T⊊V} φ_G(T), with probability at least 2/3?
cards.definitions: Here φ_G(S)=|E(S,V∖S)|/(|S|·|V∖S|), where E(S,V∖S) is the set of edges having exactly one endpoint in S. The graph is supplied explicitly by an adjacency matrix. Polynomial time is measured in bit operations on every random tape; the same algorithm and constant must work for all graphs. The zero-optimum disconnected case requires returning a zero cut. Uniform refers to equal demand for each pair of vertices, not regularity of the graph.

context_blocks.text: Uniform Sparsest Cut balances a cut’s edge boundary against the number of separated pairs. It is a basic measure of the decomposability of a graph and a major test case for approximation algorithms.

The ARV result gives an O(√log n) approximation, with a bound growing with the graph size. A constant factor would cross the remaining qualitative approximation barrier. Nonuniform pair demands, conductance normalized by volumes, and Small-Set Expansion have different targets and are not silently substituted here.

cards.title: Unconditional NP-hardness at the Goemans–Williamson Max-Cut threshold
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every rational ε with 0<ε<1−α_GW, do rationals 0<b<a≤1 with b/a<α_GW+ε exist such that distinguishing Max-Cut value at least a from value at most b is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: For a finite simple undirected graph with at least one edge, its Max-Cut value is the maximum fraction of edges crossing a bipartition. Let α_GW=min_{0<θ≤π} 2θ/(π(1−cos θ)). NP-hardness means there is a polynomial-time map from 3-CNF formulas to graphs mapping satisfiable formulas to the at-least-a case and unsatisfiable formulas to the at-most-b case. The reduction and constants may depend on ε. No Unique Games or other hardness conjecture is assumed.

context_blocks.text: The Goemans–Williamson approximation ratio is a landmark in semidefinite optimization. Matching hardness from ordinary NP-hardness would identify that ratio as an intrinsic computational threshold under P≠NP.

Known optimal hardness follows from Unique Games; it is not an unconditional NP-hardness theorem. The target deliberately concerns the reduction itself, so a conditional implication from UGC does not count as a solution. This separates the problem from the Unique Games conjecture and from improving a particular rounding algorithm.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Dasgupta’s hierarchical clustering objective
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do a universal constant C≥1 and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm exist which, for every finite undirected graph G=([n],E) with nonnegative rational edge weights w, output a rooted full binary tree T whose leaves are bijectively labeled by [n] and whose cost is at most C times the minimum cost of such a tree, where cost_G(T)=∑_{{u,v}∈E}w_{uv}|L_T(lca_T(u,v))|?
cards.definitions: Here n≥2. The least common ancestor lca_T(u,v) is the lowest common ancestor of the leaves u and v. L_T(z) is the set of leaves below node z, including a leaf itself. Every internal node has exactly two children. Weights are encoded by binary integer numerators and positive denominators; running time is polynomial in the total explicit input bit length. If all weights vanish, every tree has zero cost. The output tree is explicit. No auxiliary distance, planted model or triplet-query oracle is given.

context_blocks.text: Dasgupta’s objective makes hierarchical clustering a single optimization problem: heavily connected items pay more when they are separated high in the hierarchy. This gives a mathematically specified approximation question on arbitrary similarity graphs.

Known general guarantees and conditional hardness leave a substantial gap. The Small-Set Expansion hypothesis rules out constant-factor approximation, but that is a conditional barrier rather than an unconditional resolution. Constant guarantees with extra comparison oracles concern a different input model.

cards.title: Square-root logarithmic approximation for metric labeling
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Does a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist giving an O(√log(k+2)) approximation for every metric-labeling instance with k labels?
cards.definitions: An instance consists of a finite undirected graph G=(V,E), nonnegative rational edge weights w_uv, a metric d on [k] supplied by its rational distance matrix, and nonnegative rational assignment costs c(v,i). A labeling f:V→[k] has cost Σ_v c(v,f(v))+Σ_{uv∈E}w_uv d(f(u),f(v)). The guarantee is cost(f)≤C√log(k+2)·OPT with probability at least 2/3 for a universal C. Running time on every random tape is polynomial in the entire binary input length; k is part of the input. No restriction on the metric or graph is promised.

context_blocks.text: Metric labeling combines local assignment costs with penalties for assigning far-apart labels to neighboring vertices. It captures a broad family of classification and partitioning objectives.

General algorithms give logarithmic approximation, while the square-root logarithmic scale arises in hardness. Closing the gap would identify the approximation power of this general model. Results for a uniform, line or truncated metric leave arbitrary label metrics unresolved.

cards.title: Planted clique: can polynomial time detect a clique below the square-root scale?
cards.formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed ε∈(0,1/2), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm A whose success probability in the experiment below is at least 2/3 for every sufficiently large n, with k=⌊n^(1/2−ε)⌋.
cards.definitions: Set [n]={1,…,n}. The null distribution N_n draws a simple undirected labeled graph by including each unordered pair independently with probability 1/2. The planted distribution P_(n,k) first chooses S uniformly among all k-element subsets of [n], includes all edges inside S, and includes every other edge independently with probability 1/2. Draw b uniformly from {0,1}; draw G from N_n if b=0 and P_(n,k) if b=1. Give A the binary integers n,k and the full adjacency matrix of G, but neither b nor S. It outputs a bit b̂. Success means Pr[b̂=b], averaged over b, the graph, S when present, and A’s independent random bits. Equivalently success is (Pr_N[A=0]+Pr_P[A=1])/2. Polynomial time means at most C(n+1)^c bit operations for every input and random tape, with fixed C,c; they and A may depend on the fixed ε. The forbidden guarantee is ∃A,C,c,N ∀n≥N, success≥2/3. This is a one-graph detection problem; A may generate its own random graphs at its own computational cost. The size of S is exactly k, not an independent per-vertex planting probability. No advice, quantum computation, oracle, side information, or algorithm-family restriction is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis and a central test case for statistical–computational gaps. It asks for a clean separation between the presence of information and efficient extraction of that information; reductions transfer related assumptions to sparse estimation and latent-structure learning. Proving this formulation would in particular imply P≠NP, since a polynomial algorithm for maximum clique would distinguish the distributions.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026; no unrestricted polynomial-time solution below n^(1/2−ε) or unconditional hardness proof was identified. The exact formulation fixes constant-success detection and exactly k planted vertices. Low-degree and sum-of-squares bounds remain scoped to their models; the optimal-advantage result is conditional.

context_blocks.text: This asks whether a planted structure can be statistically obvious yet computationally inaccessible. In the specified regime, k grows as a positive power of n, while an unplanted graph has no clique of size r=⌈3 log_2 n⌉ with probability tending to one: a union bound is at most n^r·2^(−r(r−1)/2), which tends to zero. Enumerating all r-subsets therefore distinguishes the two distributions with success tending to one in quasipolynomial time n^O(log n). The obstacle is reducing that computation to polynomial time, not a lack of information in the graph.

The classical spectral algorithm of Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov recovers the hidden vertex set for every fixed positive constant times √n, with a polynomial whose exponent can depend on that constant. Recovery immediately yields detection here by checking that the reported set is a sufficiently large clique. Letting the constant shrink as n^(−ε) does not keep that analysis polynomial with a fixed exponent.

Substantial evidence comes from provable failures of general algorithmic frameworks. Barak and coauthors show that low-degree sum-of-squares relaxations assign a random graph an implausibly large clique value near √n, despite its true largest clique having only logarithmic size. This is an unconditional limitation of that relaxation. It does not rule out every algorithm allowed in this card.

Recent positive work also illustrates why an algorithmic barrier must state its model. Gheissari, Jagannath, and Xu permit local optimization to pass through vertex sets that are not cliques, penalizing missing edges. Starting from the whole graph, their procedure reaches the planted clique at a sufficiently large constant times √n. Restrictions to moves among actual cliques can fail even in easier regimes; those failures do not establish the unrestricted conjecture.

Nagda and Raghavendra obtain sharp bounds on efficient distinguishing advantage assuming planted-clique hardness. Their paper uses independent vertex planting, so the planted size fluctuates around its mean, and uses a different normalization of advantage. It strengthens consequences of a hypothesis in that related model. It is not an unconditional lower bound for the fixed-size experiment here.

The question isolates detection from stronger output requirements such as recovering every planted vertex. It also fixes the random background: arbitrary base graphs, geometric random graphs, and adversarially modified edges describe different experiments. Work on robust recovery of overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs continued in COLT 2026, but its distribution and signal regime do not settle this question.

cards.title: Does P≠NP imply a samplable NP problem outside AvgP?
cards.formal: Is the implication $\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\Longrightarrow(\mathrm{NP},\mathrm{PSamp})\nsubseteq\mathrm{AvgP}$ true? That is, assuming P≠NP, must there exist a language L∈NP and a polynomial-time samplable distribution ensemble D={Dₙ} such that no deterministic exact decider for L runs in average polynomial time under D, in the moment-based sense defined below?
cards.definitions: A sampler is one randomized Turing machine S which, given 1ⁿ, halts within q(n) steps on every random tape for a fixed polynomial q. Its output distribution Dₙ is over finite binary strings x; |x|≤q(n), and n is the ensemble parameter, not necessarily |x|. Sampling is exact with independent unbiased coin flips, and S has no advice or oracle. An exact decider A receives (1ⁿ,x), halts, and returns the membership bit of L correctly for every n and x. Write T_A(1ⁿ,x) for its running time. The pair (L,D) belongs to AvgP if there exist such an A, ε>0, C>0, and integer k≥1 with $\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\varepsilon]\le C(n+1)^k$ for every n≥1. The constants and A may depend on L and S but not on n. This moment definition is the robust Levin notion, not the requirement that the first moment itself be polynomial. The algorithm is deterministic and never gives a wrong answer; difficult inputs may take a long time. NP uses ordinary polynomially bounded certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification. Both the hard language and its sampler must be fixed across all input lengths.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This asks whether worst-case intractability necessarily survives on inputs generated by a feasible process. It is the basic bridge between the standard theory of NP-completeness and distributional complexity, and a prerequisite issue in attempts to derive useful cryptographic hardness from P≠NP alone.

importance.reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.

progress.text: Levin develops robust average-time definitions and distributional completeness; Impagliazzo and Levin extend completeness to samplable ensembles. The survey develops the moment definition and this completeness theory.

Bogdanov and Trevisan show limitations of nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP. Their result is a conditional obstruction to a reduction method, not a disproof of the unrestricted implication.
Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.5 and the revised Bogdanov–Trevisan survey explicitly ask whether P≠NP implies average-case NP hardness.

Liu and Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case reduction for an exact time-bounded Kolmogorov problem under an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. The extra hypothesis is stronger and more specific than P≠NP.

cards.status_note: The original question is explicitly open in Wigderson’s book and the revised average-case survey. Current primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no resolution from P≠NP alone was located. The card fixes deterministic exact AvgP and strict polynomial-time sampling, rather than conflating them with randomized heuristic hardness.

context_blocks.text: Worst-case hardness says that an algorithm has difficult inputs. It does not say that a feasible instance generator produces them with enough probability to obstruct average efficiency. The sampler is therefore part of the mathematical problem. It may depend on the language, but it cannot contain an uncomputable table selecting a hard input at every length.

A padding example shows why a fixed familiar distribution is insufficient. Encode a formula x as 0 followed by |x|²−1 further zeros, a separator 1, and x. Satisfiability of these padded strings remains NP-complete under polynomial reductions. Under the uniform distribution on strings of a fixed length, valid encodings are so rare that checking the format and brute-forcing the rare valid formulas has polynomial average cost. An easy uniform distribution does not remove worst-case hardness.

Levin’s moment condition makes average efficiency stable under polynomial slowdowns. If a machine is simulated with its running time raised to a fixed power, a correspondingly smaller positive moment still suffices. This prevents the answer from depending on an incidental choice of machine representation. Exact computation with this runtime guarantee differs from a heuristic allowed to give incorrect answers on a small fraction of inputs.

Distributional completeness is already available: Impagliazzo and Levin extend the theory to polynomial-time samplable ensembles. Completeness identifies a common average-case target; it does not prove that this target is hard from P≠NP.

There are barriers for nonadaptive oracle reductions from worst-case NP hardness to average-case NP hardness: the relevant reductions would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such a barrier leaves other proof mechanisms open. Recent reductions for specific time-bounded Kolmogorov problems use additional assumptions or specific forms of hardness, so they do not supply the implication on this card.

cards.title: The computational threshold for dense tensor PCA
cards.formal: For every fixed integer k≥3, rational ε with 0<ε<(k−2)/4, and rational c∈(0,1), is the following impossibility statement true? No uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm, given the finite-precision observation of Y=n^{k/4−ε}v^{⊗k}+Z specified below, achieves |⟨u,v⟩|≥c with probability at least 2/3 for every sufficiently large dimension n, where v is uniform on the unit sphere in R^n and the n^k ordered entries of Z are independent N(0,1) variables.
cards.definitions: The experiment draws v, Z and the algorithm’s random bits independently. For an ordered tuple (i₁,…,i_k)∈{1,…,n}^k, the signal entry is n^{k/4−ε}v_{i₁}⋯v_{i_k}. Noise is not pre-symmetrized and each entry has variance one. To give polynomial time a precise bit-model meaning, for n≥2 set b=⌈10k log₂n⌉ and Q_b(x)=2^{−b}⌊2^b max(−2^b,min(x,2^b))⌋. The input consists of n and all entries Q_b(Y_{i₁,…,i_k}), represented as signed dyadic rationals with O(log n) bits each. This fixed rounding convention is an explicit finite-precision version of the usual Gaussian-model question. An algorithm may depend on the fixed constants k, ε and c, but is one probabilistic Turing machine for all n, with worst-case running time polynomial in n on every input and random tape. For fixed k this is polynomial in the input size. It outputs a nonzero rational vector w, interpreted as the unit vector u=w/‖w‖₂; zero or invalid outputs fail. Success is the event |⟨w,v⟩|≥c‖w‖₂. The algorithm receives no side information about v, informative initial vector, or additional independent observations. The probability averages over the spike, noise and internal randomness. Absolute correlation makes the target invariant under the unavoidable sign ambiguity when k is even.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed (k,ε,c) in the stated ranges, each such polynomial-time algorithm has success probability below 2/3 for arbitrarily large n; or refute this by giving one fixed triple and one algorithm that succeeds with probability at least 2/3 for all sufficiently large n. Proving failure only for low-degree polynomials, a chosen iterative method, or a different spike prior does not prove the full assertion. An improvement by logarithmic factors at n^{k/4} does not supply the fixed power saving n^ε requested here.
cards.why: Determine whether the canonical statistical–computational gap for a dense Gaussian tensor persists against all polynomial-time recovery algorithms.

importance.reason: A central average-case inference problem linking tensor algorithms, statistical thresholds, low-degree methods and computational hardness.

progress.text: Montanari–Richard introduce and analyze the spiked tensor model, exhibiting a gap between information-theoretic recovery and the analyzed polynomial-time methods.

Wu–Zhou sharpen the analysis and stopping rule for randomly initialized power iteration; its threshold improves by a polylogarithmic factor.
Ding–Gu–Liu–Fang improve stochastic-gradient guarantees in a multiple-observation model; the even-order bound reaches the familiar conjectured computational scale.
Fu–Sohn establish low-degree estimation bounds for independent-coordinate priors, with the predicted degree–signal dependence and an additional technical restriction on degree.

cards.status_note: The May 2026 low-degree paper retains the conjectured gap for unrestricted algorithms and distinguishes spherical from independent-coordinate priors. The 2024 power-iteration and October 2025 stochastic-gradient improvements concern particular methods and do not provide a fixed-power improvement below n^{k/4}. No full resolution found through 11 September 2026. The card explicitly fixes a finite-precision bit model; restricted lower bounds in the standard unrounded model are evidence, not a proof for all algorithms here.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary principal component analysis looks for a hidden direction in a noisy matrix. Tensor PCA asks the analogous question when observations have three or more indices. Here the clean signal has rank one: every entry is a product of coordinates of the same hidden unit vector. Gaussian noise obscures those products. The goal is only a constant correlation with the direction, much weaker than estimating every coordinate accurately.

For fixed tensor order, information-theoretic recovery in the standard Gaussian model becomes possible at a signal scale of order √n. Montanari and Richard established the basic statistical-versus-computational distinction while studying tensor unfolding, power iteration and message-passing methods. Their noise normalization differs from the variance-one convention used in this card; their constant statistical threshold corresponds to order √n here.

Known polynomial-time methods reach signal strength around n^{k/4}, up to factors that do not change this leading exponent. Wu and Zhou’s 2024 introduction records both this algorithmic scale and the conjectured gap from √n. The interval for ε deliberately places our target strictly between them: λ/√n=n^{(k−2)/4−ε} grows without bound. There is therefore ample statistical signal in the usual model, while efficient recovery remains unproved.

For example, at order four and ε=1/8, the observation contains n^4 noisy numbers and signal strength n^{7/8}. The statistical scale is n^{1/2}, and the conjectured efficient scale is n. A polynomial-time algorithm below that latter scale would have to exploit structure that current threshold evidence misses. Merely reading all n^4 entries is allowed: the question concerns computation polynomial in the complete input, not a sublinear-access restriction.

Low-degree polynomial estimators provide one rigorous way to test proposed computational barriers. Kunisky, Moore and Wein establish the predicted degree-versus-signal tradeoff for detection with a spherical spike and derive a matching reconstruction lower bound for odd tensor orders. Their reconstruction theorem is specifically for odd orders; they explain that even orders require a sign-invariant estimand such as vvᵀ and additional work. Detection and recovery are separate tasks, and a detection lower bound should not silently be relabelled as their reconstruction theorem.

Fu and Sohn’s May 2026 preprint advances low-degree estimation bounds for tensor PCA with independent, mean-zero, variance-one spike coordinates and bounded moments. Its general-prior theorem controls estimation of fixed products of coordinates and obtains the predicted signal-versus-degree scaling within a stated degree range. Independent-coordinate priors are different from a vector conditioned to have unit norm. The result strengthens evidence for the computational gap without establishing an unrestricted polynomial-time lower bound for this card’s spherical prior.

Some recent algorithmic improvements resolve narrower conjectures. Wu and Zhou lower the threshold for randomly initialized power iteration by a polylogarithmic factor. Ding, Gu, Liu and Fang obtain improved guarantees for an overparameterized stochastic-gradient method using multiple independent observations. For even order, their stated sample-signal condition reaches the familiar n^{k/4} scale after averaging the observations. Neither result supplies the fixed-power improvement below that scale demanded here.

The rounding convention prevents an ambiguity about algorithms operating on exact Gaussian real numbers. Each coordinate is given with logarithmically many bits. Outside the clipping event, the total rounding error in Euclidean norm across the tensor is at most n^{k/2}2^{−b}, an extremely small inverse power of n; clipping has vanishing probability. This is a specified computational model, rather than an assertion that every exact-real algorithm automatically transfers to it. Likewise, polynomial-estimator theorems for unrounded observations do not by themselves cover arbitrary algorithms that process rounded entries.

A resolution would clarify whether a simple, highly symmetric random model can hide statistically recoverable information from every efficient algorithm. A successful method would challenge a widely used picture of algorithmic thresholds. A full impossibility proof would require a complexity argument beyond the restricted algorithm families currently understood. Both outcomes would inform how computational hardness assumptions are formulated for inference problems.

cards.title: The computational Kesten–Stigum threshold for sparse community recovery
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed integer q≥5, fixed rational constants a>b>0 satisfying (a−b)²<q(a+(q−1)b), a constant δ>0, and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every sufficiently large n, A weakly recovers the communities of the symmetric stochastic block model SBM(n,q,a,b), with expected overlap at least 1/q+δ?
cards.definitions: Generate the hidden labels σ₁,…,σₙ independently and uniformly from [q]={1,…,q}. Conditional on these labels, each unordered pair of distinct vertices is independently an edge with probability a/n if its labels agree and b/n otherwise. Thus the graph is simple and undirected; take n≥a. Equal prior probabilities make communities asymptotically balanced, but their sizes are not conditioned to equal n/q. The algorithm receives this one graph and knows q,a,b; it receives no planted labels or auxiliary samples. It outputs a label vector σ̂∈[q]ⁿ. Define overlap(σ̂,σ)=max over permutations π of [q] of n⁻¹Σᵢ 1{σ̂ᵢ=π(σᵢ)}. The expectation in the question is over labels, graph edges and the algorithm’s random bits. Weak recovery means a fixed positive advantage over the limiting chance baseline 1/q. Running time is worst-case polynomial in n on a standard bit model, for every graph and random tape; the algorithm and polynomial exponent may depend on the fixed parameters but not on n. Put d=(a+(q−1)b)/q and θ=(a−b)/(a+(q−1)b). The strict inequality is dθ²<1, below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. All three model parameters remain constant as n grows.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer must exhibit one fixed parameter choice below the threshold and prove the stated polynomial running time and nonvanishing expected overlap for all sufficiently large n. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm at every fixed parameter choice in the formulation. Recovery with unlimited computation does not answer the question. An algorithm with q growing with n, a result only above the threshold, or a lower bound conditional on an unproved computational hypothesis is partial progress. The question does not impose an extra promise of information-theoretic recoverability: any positive algorithmic example automatically has that property.
cards.why: Determine whether the canonical local signal threshold is a true barrier for every efficient algorithm in a basic model of network inference.

importance.reason: A central, sharply parameterized computational-versus-statistical gap linking sparse random graphs, inference, message passing and average-case complexity.

cards.status_note: Efficient recovery above the threshold and information-theoretic recovery below it in suitable fixed-q assortative regimes are proved. The checked fixed-community computational lower bound remains conditional on an unproved low-degree conjecture. Growing-community algorithms in the August 2026 revision concern a different quantifier regime. No unconditional settlement of this precise fixed-q question found through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Community detection asks whether the edges of a network reveal an underlying partition. Here every vertex has the same expected degree, regardless of its group. Consequently, sorting vertices by degree cannot directly identify their communities. The signal is in the pattern of connections between vertices, and each vertex has only a constant expected number of observations even as the network grows.

The target is deliberately much weaker than recovering every label. A constant-degree graph has many isolated vertices, whose memberships cannot be inferred from their incident edges. Weak recovery asks only for a fixed improvement over random guessing on average. Permuting all community names must be allowed: renaming the hidden groups changes neither the graph distribution nor the quality of an inferred partition.

The quantity dθ² compares the growth in the number of observed neighbours with the decay of label information along an edge. In a local tree approximation, d describes branching and θ describes how much a child’s label remembers its parent’s label. This explains why the value one is a natural boundary for algorithms based on propagation of small correlations. It does not by itself prove an impossibility result for algorithms that use the whole graph.

Abbe and Sandon prove efficient recovery above this boundary for every fixed number of communities. Their method uses an acyclic form of belief propagation and addresses the effect of cycles in the finite graph. This supplies the algorithmic side of the proposed threshold. The question asks whether a qualitatively different method can succeed strictly below it in the assortative case a>b.

There really are parameters for which the graph contains useful information below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. Banks, Moore, Neeman and Netrapalli establish such regimes for at least eleven groups in the assortative model. Their recovery argument permits exponential computation, searching over sufficiently plausible partitions. Their five-group statement concerns the disassortative case, where between-group edges are more likely; that is a different parameter range from this card.

This produces a concrete computational-versus-statistical puzzle. The missing labels are not intrinsically unidentifiable everywhere below the boundary, yet known efficient methods do not recover them throughout the information-theoretically possible region. An affirmative answer to this card would refute the universal fixed-community barrier with a single parameter example. A negative answer would establish that the obstruction is computational wherever recovery is statistically possible.

Ding, Hua, Slot and Steurer give conditional evidence in 2025. In their parameterized symmetric model, a low-degree conjecture implies a strong computational lower bound for recovery below the threshold by a fixed margin. Their recovery definition uses correlation with the centred membership matrix. The result is a reduction from a conjecture about testing to recovery hardness, not an unconditional exclusion of polynomial-time algorithms. Its model and hypothesis restrictions matter when applying it to a particular choice of a,b.

The precise conjecture in that paper also matters. Its bounded test functions must have expectation bounded below under the planted distribution. The authors explain that a broader earlier version was refuted using rare events. Thus citing a generic “low-degree conjecture” without stating that a hypothesis remains unproved would erase both the conditional nature of the result and an actual correction in the underlying evidence.

A 2026 revision of work by Chin, Mossel, Sohn and Wein gives efficient recovery below the usual boundary when the number of communities grows sufficiently quickly, in particular in a regime above √n. This is an important warning against treating the threshold as universal over every block model. Here q is fixed before n tends to infinity. Even a very large fixed q eventually lies below √n, so the growing-community algorithm does not supply the fixed-parameter example requested.

Settling this problem would test whether a threshold suggested by local propagation describes all efficient global algorithms in a basic random graph model. A new algorithm would identify exploitable structure missed by the familiar threshold calculation. A rigorous barrier would give a particularly clean example in which unlimited inference and efficient inference have different capabilities, with the data distribution specified by only three constants.

cards.title: Can random 3-SAT at constant density be refuted in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer C≥6 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that A never outputs UNSAT on any satisfiable 3-CNF formula, and Pr[A(F)=UNSAT]→1 as n→∞ for F drawn from R_3(n,Cn)? The probability is over both the formula and A’s independent random bits.
cards.definitions: For n≥3, R_3(n,m) is the distribution on ordered lists of m clauses obtained independently with replacement. Each clause selects a uniformly random three-element subset of {1,…,n} and independently negates each of its three variables with probability 1/2. Each clause is their disjunction; the formula is the conjunction of the list, with duplicate clauses permitted. On every input A outputs UNSAT or UNKNOWN. Soundness is exact: for every satisfiable formula and every random tape A returns UNKNOWN. Its time is bounded by a fixed polynomial in the explicit binary input length on every input and every random tape, including adversarial formulas; variable names are binary integers and n is part of the encoding. A may use only fresh independent fair random bits and has no advice or external oracle. The constant C, the machine, and the time polynomial are chosen before n. The probability limit means that for every η>0 there is n0 such that the probability is at least 1−η for all n≥n0. There is no requirement to use a specified refutation proof system: a sound decision procedure certifying unsatisfiability suffices. Restricting the existential choice to integers C≥6 loses no larger constant-density regime, since an algorithm at a smaller density can run on the corresponding prefix of the random clause list.

context_blocks.text: At a sufficiently large fixed clause density, a random 3-CNF formula is unsatisfiable with probability approaching one. That fact alone does not give a sound algorithm for a particular input: a procedure that always announces unsatisfiability would incorrectly reject satisfiable adversarial formulas. The question is whether an efficient algorithm can recognize almost all random instances while retaining exact soundness on every satisfiable instance.

The random distribution and the algorithmic quantifiers have different roles. A is constrained on all inputs, but its success guarantee applies to the stated distribution. C is an absolute constant, so success only at a density growing with n does not meet the target. Likewise, proving that short certificates exist does not automatically yield an algorithm that finds them.

Allen, O’Donnell and Witmer define refutation as a sound UNSAT-or-fail procedure and develop refutation algorithms for random constraint satisfaction problems. They distinguish this task from planted-instance detection and from strong refutation, which certifies that every assignment violates a positive fraction of constraints. These distinctions determine which hardness assumptions and consequences apply.

Feige’s random-3-SAT hypothesis is often presented in a stronger gap formulation. For example, Barak’s formulation requires soundness even on nearly satisfiable formulas. This card records the exact-satisfiability, constant-density refutation question requested in the proposal; it does not identify that formulation with every version called Feige’s hypothesis. The gap formulation is documented as related context.

Chan, d’Orsi and Xu’s 2026 work generalizes density, sum-of-squares degree and refutation-strength tradeoffs for random CSPs. Its broader predicate model is not a polynomial-time, constant-density solution of this random-3-SAT target. The question remains a distinct counterpart to the catalogue’s planted-clique detection problem.

cards.why: Separate the typical absence of satisfying assignments from the computational ability to certify that absence soundly.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.

importance.reason: A foundational average-case refutation problem with documented connections to proof complexity, learning and approximation. It supplies a different average-case task from planted recovery or detection. The exact-satisfiability variant is recorded without importing consequences of stronger gap hypotheses.

cards.title: Does average-case NP hardness imply infinitely-often one-way functions?
cards.formal: Does $\mathrm{DistNP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{HeurBPP}$ imply the existence of a polynomial-time computable function f with the following property? For every probabilistic polynomial-time inverter I and every constant c>0, infinitely many lengths n satisfy $\Pr[|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)]<n^{-c}$, where $x\sim U(\{0,1\}^n)$ and $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$. The probability includes inverter randomness. This card fixes the infinitely-often security convention used by the cited characterization.
cards.why: It asks whether distributional hardness alone suffices for basic cryptography: a central connection between average-case complexity and cryptographic constructions.

progress.text: The revised paper characterizes the remaining obstruction by the gap between approximation factors $\ell^{1-o(1)}$ and $O(\ell)$ for minimum-description-length agnostic learning. Here $\ell$ is advice complexity of sampling. The original April version states a different quantitative claim.

cards.review_note: The earlier shorthand omitted the infinitely-often qualifier. This version fixes it to match Theorem 1.5 of revision 1. The all-sufficiently-large-length variant must not be silently identified with this statement. Importance is editorial and proofs have not been independently audited.

context_blocks.text: Hardness of deciding typical instances and hardness of finding preimages are different requirements. The assumption P ≠ NP alone is weaker and belongs to a separate existing question.

An average-case decision problem asks an algorithm to classify instances drawn from a specified distribution. A one-way function creates a different experiment: sample an input, reveal its efficiently computed image, and ask an adversary to find any valid preimage. The sampling process and the form of the required answer both matter.

A reduction has to turn the first kind of difficulty into the second while preserving efficient generation and a meaningful success probability. It cannot simply use a hard yes/no question as a function and assume its inverse is hard. The question is whether some average-case hardness can exist without yielding the basic inversion obstacle on which one-way-function cryptography is built.

cards.definitions: DistNP consists of pairs (L,D) with L in NP and D_n a polynomial-time samplable distribution on n-bit inputs. Such a pair is in HeurBPP if a single randomized algorithm A runs in time polynomial in n and 1/delta and, for every n and $0<\delta<1$, at least a $1-\delta$ fraction of x drawn from D_n have $\Pr[A(x,\delta)=L(x)]\ge2/3$. The output is a decision bit. Infinitely-often security is weaker than requiring negligible inversion probability at all sufficiently large lengths; the latter is a distinct stronger target.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication under the two explicit distributional and security definitions, or prove that average-case NP hardness can hold while every polynomial-time function fails that infinitely-often inversion guarantee. A result only about an oracle world does not settle the unrelativized implication.

importance.reason: Links average-case NP hardness to the existence of a basic cryptographic primitive; resolving it would clarify the foundations of complexity-based cryptography.

cards.title: Polynomial smoothed complexity of FLIP for Max-Cut
cards.formal: Are there absolute constants C,a,b>0 such that, for every n≥1, every simple undirected graph G on n vertices, every φ≥1/2 and every collection of independent edge-weight distributions supported on [−1,1] with probability densities bounded by φ, the expected length of the longest strictly improving single-vertex-flip path is at most C(n+1)^a(1+φ)^b?
cards.why: A flagship unresolved explanation of why a canonical PLS local-search algorithm works efficiently on perturbed inputs.
cards.status_note: The ESA 2024 source explicitly retains the arbitrary-graph problem. Searches for subsequent work through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of this expected longest-path target. The general high-probability upper bound and the smoothed 3-FLIP lower bound were separated from the required guarantee. Proofs have not been independently audited.
cards.review_note: Fixed the source’s signed [-1,1] bounded-density model and one-shot independent sampling. Made expectation of the longest path, arbitrary initial cuts, strict improvement and iteration cost explicit. Preserved the expected-time target; did not replace it by a tail bound or a choice of pivot rule.

progress.text: Theorem 1.1 gives the general upper bound φn^{O(√log n)} with high probability, controlling every directed path in the improvement graph.
The sparse-graph theorem gives polynomial expected and high-probability bounds for arboricity O(log^{1−δ}n), with any fixed δ∈(0,1]. The paper retains arbitrary graphs as an open case.
The author manuscript gives a smoothed superpolynomial lower bound for 3-FLIP and unperturbed exponential single-FLIP examples; both have a different scope from this target.
