cards.definitions: The graph and one Lebesgue-measurable density f_e for each edge are chosen adversarially before the random weights. Each f_e is nonnegative, integrates to 1 on [−1,1], and is at most φ almost everywhere; weights w_e are sampled independently once from these densities and then held fixed. They may be negative and need not be identically distributed. A cut is a subset S⊆V, with value W_w(S)=Σ_{uv∈E: exactly one of u,v lies in S} w_uv. A legal step replaces S by S△{v} for one vertex v, and requires a strictly larger cut value. Define L(G,w) as the largest number of steps in any such path, maximized over all starting cuts and all choices of improving vertices after w is known; set L=0 if there is no step. There are finitely many cuts and strict improvement prevents revisiting one, so L≤2^n−1 and its expectation is well-defined. The expectation is over w alone, with the maximum over paths inside it. The resource counted is improving steps, not the bit cost of exact real arithmetic or of sampling distributions. The target concerns all graphs and all allowed densities with one common polynomial. A run ends at a single-flip local maximum, which need not maximize cut value globally.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound on E_w[L(G,w)], or prove its logical negation by exhibiting admissible families that exceed every such polynomial. A bound for selected graph classes or for one favorable pivot rule does not establish the proposition. A rare long path or an unperturbed worst-case instance alone does not refute an expected bound under these density constraints.

context_blocks.title: What FLIP improves
context_blocks.text: The procedure repeatedly moves a vertex to the opposite side when this increases the weight crossing the cut. Different choices can produce different paths, so the question controls the longest one. This includes starting cuts and choices made after seeing the sampled weights, rather than relying on a particular implementation to avoid a bad path.

context_blocks.title: Local optimality has a different goal
context_blocks.text: Consider a four-cycle 1–2–3–4–1 with weights 0.9 on edges 12 and 34 and weights 1 on edges 23 and 41. The cut {1,2} has weight 2, and moving any single vertex decreases it by 0.1. Nevertheless, the alternating cut {1,3} has weight 3.8. Fast termination here would mean finding a state with no improving single move, without asserting that FLIP finds a global maximum.

context_blocks.title: What the smoothing parameter permits
context_blocks.text: The adversary chooses the graph and the distributions, while independent draws supply the randomness. Density bounded by φ prevents a distribution from putting too much probability in an arbitrarily short interval: an interval of length h has probability at most φh. Larger φ permits more concentrated weights, and the requested running-time bound may grow polynomially with φ.

context_blocks.title: Known bounds cover only part of the target
context_blocks.text: The general-graph theorem of Chen and coauthors gives φn^{O(√log n)} steps with high probability, uniformly over improving paths. Schwartzman proves polynomial expected length when arboricity is O(log^{1−δ}n) for fixed δ>0; arboricity is the minimum number of forests needed to partition the edges. This includes sparse graph classes but not arbitrary graphs. The expectation requirement matters: a high-probability statement by itself does not bound the contribution of a long tail.

context_blocks.title: A nearby negative result uses larger moves
context_blocks.text: Michel and Scott show superpolynomial smoothed behavior for 3-FLIP, where a step may move up to three vertices together. Their single-FLIP exponential examples instead concern the setting without random perturbations. Neither statement refutes polynomial expected length for the single-vertex, independently perturbed model here.

cards.context:
The procedure repeatedly moves a vertex to the opposite side when this increases the weight crossing the cut. Different choices can produce different paths, so the question controls the longest one. This includes starting cuts and choices made after seeing the sampled weights, rather than relying on a particular implementation to avoid a bad path.

Consider a four-cycle 1–2–3–4–1 with weights 0.9 on edges 12 and 34 and weights 1 on edges 23 and 41. The cut {1,2} has weight 2, and moving any single vertex decreases it by 0.1. Nevertheless, the alternating cut {1,3} has weight 3.8. Fast termination here would mean finding a state with no improving single move, without asserting that FLIP finds a global maximum.

The adversary chooses the graph and the distributions, while independent draws supply the randomness. Density bounded by φ prevents a distribution from putting too much probability in an arbitrarily short interval: an interval of length h has probability at most φh. Larger φ permits more concentrated weights, and the requested running-time bound may grow polynomially with φ.

The general-graph theorem of Chen and coauthors gives φn^{O(√log n)} steps with high probability, uniformly over improving paths. Schwartzman proves polynomial expected length when arboricity is O(log^{1−δ}n) for fixed δ>0; arboricity is the minimum number of forests needed to partition the edges. This includes sparse graph classes but not arbitrary graphs. The expectation requirement matters: a high-probability statement by itself does not bound the contribution of a long tail.

Michel and Scott show superpolynomial smoothed behavior for 3-FLIP, where a step may move up to three vertices together. Their single-FLIP exponential examples instead concern the setting without random perturbations. Neither statement refutes polynomial expected length for the single-vertex, independently perturbed model here.

cards.title: Constant adaptivity gap for influence maximization with full feedback
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that OPT_adaptive(G,p,k)≤C·OPT_nonadaptive(G,p,k) for every independent-cascade influence instance under full-adoption feedback?
cards.definitions: The input is any finite directed graph, an independent retention probability p_e∈[0,1] for each edge, and a budget 1≤k≤|V|. Sample a live-edge subgraph once. A seed activates all vertices reachable from it along live edges. A nonadaptive strategy selects at most k seeds before observing the subgraph. An adaptive strategy selects seeds sequentially, observing after each choice the resulting activated set and the outcomes of edges explored by its completed cascade. Both objectives maximize the expected total number of activated vertices over strategies with no computational restriction. The expectation is over the live-edge graph and strategy coins. Failed transmissions into vertices already active reveal no additional state.

context_blocks.text: Feedback may allow later interventions to respond to the success of earlier ones. The adaptivity gap measures the value of that information, independently of the difficulty of finding an optimal strategy.

cards.title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with Δ+2 colours
cards.formal: Do absolute constants C,c>0 exist such that, for every finite simple n-vertex graph G with maximum degree Δ and every integer q≥Δ+2, the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper q-colourings has total-variation mixing time t_mix(1/4)≤Cn^c?
cards.definitions: Let n≥1 and Ω={σ:V(G)→[q] : σ(u)≠σ(v) for every edge uv}. Colours are labelled; unused colours are allowed. At each discrete step choose v uniformly from V(G), then choose a colour uniformly from [q]\{σ(u):u∈N(v)} and assign it to v, leaving all other vertices unchanged. The current colour is among the available choices. Let P be this transition matrix and π the uniform distribution on Ω. Define t_mix(1/4)=min{t∈Z_{≥0}: max_{σ∈Ω} (1/2)Σ_{τ∈Ω}|P^t(σ,τ)−π(τ)|≤1/4}. This counts individual vertex updates, not sweeps or bit operations. The constants C,c must be independent of n, Δ, q and G. The initial proper colouring is arbitrary, and the graph has no girth, treewidth or randomness promise. This card fixes a uniform polynomial bound across degrees, rather than leaving the exponent’s parameter dependence implicit.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The general-graph Δ+2 conjecture remains open in the checked sources. August 2026 results improve restricted-girth regimes with fixed relative slack; they do not establish the universal additive-two bound.

context_blocks.text: A proper colouring is easy to construct greedily with this many colours. Sampling one nearly uniformly is a different task: a deterministic rule can strongly favour a small part of the solution space. Glauber dynamics is an appealing candidate because every update uses only a vertex and its neighbours, yet repeated local changes must reproduce the global distribution. The inherited paper states the conjecture and proves it for particular graph classes.

The threshold Δ+2 has a concrete role. On a clique with Δ+1 vertices and exactly Δ+1 colours, every vertex sees all other colours in its neighbourhood. No vertex can change colour, so each proper colouring is a separate absorbing state. With at least Δ+2 colours, the single-vertex chain is irreducible on every graph and converges to the uniform distribution. The unresolved issue is how long this convergence takes.

Connectivity of the recolouring graph is insufficient to control that time. A walk may need to cross a narrow passage between two large collections of colourings. Even short paths between every pair do not show that a random walk finds the appropriate passages often enough. The card therefore asks for a distributional guarantee from the worst starting colouring, rather than a bound on the number of recolourings in an intelligently chosen path.

The update convention matters when comparing sources. A second standard version proposes a colour uniformly from the entire palette and rejects it if a neighbour uses it. This is the Metropolis version used in several cited papers. Its off-diagonal transition probabilities and the heat-bath probabilities differ by a factor between 1 and q/(q−Δ). That factor is at most 1+Δ/2 in the present range, so the distinction is relevant to sharp runtime statements but does not create an exponential gap between their polynomial-mixing questions.

The early general-graph milestones were Jerrum’s q>2Δ regime and Vigoda’s improvement to roughly 11Δ/6. The latter used a flip chain that interchanges two colours on a small connected bichromatic component, followed by a comparison with single-vertex dynamics. Chen and coauthors subsequently crossed the 11/6 threshold by a small constant improvement. The 2026 ICALP paper retains Δ+2 as a conjecture, including its Glauber-dynamics version.

Carlson–Vigoda’s October 2024 revision gives a substantial further improvement. Theorem 1.1 assumes Δ≥125 and q≥1.809Δ and proves O(n log n) mixing for the flip chain. Comparison gives polynomial mixing for Glauber dynamics in that regime. Their optimal O(n log n) Glauber corollary has a constant depending on Δ and q; it is stated for fixed parameters. The headline coefficient should therefore not be read as an unrestricted optimal-time theorem for all degrees.

Graph structure can bring the colour threshold much closer to the target. Heinrich proves n^{O(tw(G)^3)} mixing with q≥Δ+2, so bounded treewidth is covered even when maximum degree is unbounded. For chordal graphs, the proved regime instead uses q≥(1+ε)(Δ+1) for a fixed positive ε. Letting treewidth grow with n, or substituting ε that shrinks with Δ, does not give the uniform statement in this card.

There was further progress during 2026. Jain–Mizgerd–Vigoda prove O_δ(n log n) mixing for the Metropolis chain when q≥(1+δ)Δ, Δ is sufficiently large in terms of fixed δ>0, and the graph has sufficiently large girth. Their August 27 revision improves the required girth from eleven to seven. This is stronger than the original April abstract, but still excludes general graphs and does not establish additive slack of only two colours.

Chen–Liu’s August 26 preprint reaches girth at least five in the same fixed-relative-slack regime for heat-bath dynamics. Its Theorem 1 proves spectral gap Ω_δ(1/n) and mixing time O_δ(n² log q+n log(1/ε)); the sharper O_δ(n log n) consequence requires degree bounded in terms of δ. Both the girth restriction and the dependence on δ matter. Taking δ=2/Δ is not justified by a theorem that first fixes δ and then requires sufficiently large Δ.

cards.context:
A proper colouring is easy to construct greedily with this many colours. Sampling one nearly uniformly is a different task: a deterministic rule can strongly favour a small part of the solution space. Glauber dynamics is an appealing candidate because every update uses only a vertex and its neighbours, yet repeated local changes must reproduce the global distribution. The inherited paper states the conjecture and proves it for particular graph classes.

The threshold Δ+2 has a concrete role. On a clique with Δ+1 vertices and exactly Δ+1 colours, every vertex sees all other colours in its neighbourhood. No vertex can change colour, so each proper colouring is a separate absorbing state. With at least Δ+2 colours, the single-vertex chain is irreducible on every graph and converges to the uniform distribution. The unresolved issue is how long this convergence takes.

Connectivity of the recolouring graph is insufficient to control that time. A walk may need to cross a narrow passage between two large collections of colourings. Even short paths between every pair do not show that a random walk finds the appropriate passages often enough. The card therefore asks for a distributional guarantee from the worst starting colouring, rather than a bound on the number of recolourings in an intelligently chosen path.

The update convention matters when comparing sources. A second standard version proposes a colour uniformly from the entire palette and rejects it if a neighbour uses it. This is the Metropolis version used in several cited papers. Its off-diagonal transition probabilities and the heat-bath probabilities differ by a factor between 1 and q/(q−Δ). That factor is at most 1+Δ/2 in the present range, so the distinction is relevant to sharp runtime statements but does not create an exponential gap between their polynomial-mixing questions.

The early general-graph milestones were Jerrum’s q>2Δ regime and Vigoda’s improvement to roughly 11Δ/6. The latter used a flip chain that interchanges two colours on a small connected bichromatic component, followed by a comparison with single-vertex dynamics. Chen and coauthors subsequently crossed the 11/6 threshold by a small constant improvement. The 2026 ICALP paper retains Δ+2 as a conjecture, including its Glauber-dynamics version.

Carlson–Vigoda’s October 2024 revision gives a substantial further improvement. Theorem 1.1 assumes Δ≥125 and q≥1.809Δ and proves O(n log n) mixing for the flip chain. Comparison gives polynomial mixing for Glauber dynamics in that regime. Their optimal O(n log n) Glauber corollary has a constant depending on Δ and q; it is stated for fixed parameters. The headline coefficient should therefore not be read as an unrestricted optimal-time theorem for all degrees.

Graph structure can bring the colour threshold much closer to the target. Heinrich proves n^{O(tw(G)^3)} mixing with q≥Δ+2, so bounded treewidth is covered even when maximum degree is unbounded. For chordal graphs, the proved regime instead uses q≥(1+ε)(Δ+1) for a fixed positive ε. Letting treewidth grow with n, or substituting ε that shrinks with Δ, does not give the uniform statement in this card.

There was further progress during 2026. Jain–Mizgerd–Vigoda prove O_δ(n log n) mixing for the Metropolis chain when q≥(1+δ)Δ, Δ is sufficiently large in terms of fixed δ>0, and the graph has sufficiently large girth. Their August 27 revision improves the required girth from eleven to seven. This is stronger than the original April abstract, but still excludes general graphs and does not establish additive slack of only two colours.

Its Theorem 1 proves spectral gap Ω_δ(1/n) and mixing time O_δ(n² log q+n log(1/ε)); the sharper O_δ(n log n) consequence requires degree bounded in terms of δ. Both the girth restriction and the dependence on δ matter. Taking δ=2/Δ is not justified by a theorem that first fixes δ and then requires sufficiently large Δ.

Its algorithms for equitable or mildly skewed colourings therefore address a separate sampling problem. They provide useful context for why global constraints complicate local sampling, while explicitly leaving the unconstrained Δ+2 conjecture open.

cards.definitions: Ω(a,b) is the set of matrices M∈{0,1}^{r×s} with Σ_j M_ij=a_i and Σ_i M_ij=b_j. The state space is promised nonempty; no restriction on density or balance is imposed. At each discrete step, stay put with probability 1/2. Otherwise choose uniformly an unordered pair of distinct rows and independently an unordered pair of distinct columns. If their 2×2 submatrix is ((1,0),(0,1)) or ((0,1),(1,0)), replace it by the other pattern; otherwise stay put. If r<2 or s<2, the state space is a singleton and each step stays put. P denotes this transition matrix and π the uniform measure on Ω. Define t_mix(1/4)=min{t∈ℕ: max_{M∈Ω} (1/2)Σ_{N∈Ω}|P^t(M,N)−1/|Ω||≤1/4}, with value +∞ if the set is empty. Time counts attempted transitions, including stays. The maximum is over every initial state. The constants are independent of r,s and all margins; preprocessing, bit costs and sampling algorithms using other transitions are not part of this mixing-time question.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove one universal bound K(r+s)^c for all feasible margins in the specified lazy chain, or prove that its worst-case mixing time is not bounded by any polynomial in r+s. A proof confined to regular or stable margins, a different chain, or average initial states does not settle the full target.

context_blocks.text: Status update: Fu, Qin and Wang’s July 2026 revision claims a solution for this exact lazy binary-matrix chain. Theorem 2.2 gives t_mix(1/4)≤binom(r,2)binom(s,2)(rs ln 2+ln 4), which implies a universal polynomial bound in r+s. The transition probabilities and scope were compared with this card. The proof was not independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

A binary matrix can describe which species occur at which sites, or which vertices are adjacent across the two sides of a bipartite graph. Fixing its row and column sums preserves the activity of every individual row and column. Sampling uniformly from all matrices with those same margins provides a baseline for asking whether additional patterns are unusual, without confusing them with the already-fixed totals.

The elementary move preserves every margin. Replacing [[1,0],[0,1]] by [[0,1],[1,0]] changes where four entries lie while leaving each involved row sum and column sum unchanged. For a 2×2 matrix with all margins equal to one there are exactly two states. The chain stays or switches with equal probability, so one attempted transition already gives the uniform distribution. Larger instances may have many possible rectangles, most of which are not switchable.

Every allowed transition has the same probability as its reverse, making the uniform distribution stationary. Feasible binary matrices with the same margins are connected by switches, and the explicit probability of staying removes periodicity. These facts establish eventual convergence. Rapid mixing asks for a bound on how long the worst initial state can remain far from uniform; connectivity alone need not give a small bound.

Earlier theorems establish rapid mixing under additional structure. The unified approach handles P-stable degree-sequence families: roughly, small perturbations of the prescribed degrees do not create more than polynomially many times as many realizations. Such results cover broad families while retaining a hypothesis absent from the universal question. An efficient algorithm that merely finds one feasible realization would address a different task.

The inherited 2018 reference compares the switch chain with Curveball, which resamples relationships across a pair of rows using a larger move. Faster practical movement does not by itself prove a polynomial worst-case bound. A theorem about another transition rule must include the appropriate chain comparison before it can answer this card’s fixed-chain question.

The authors also supply a Lean formalization repository and identify its closed main theorem. This review checked that the artifact is linked by the paper and author, but did not build it or audit the correspondence of its definitions and theorem dependencies. The presence of a formalization is recorded as evidence, not as an independent machine verification performed by this catalogue.

The question is specifically the bipartite, zero-one matrix case. Integer-valued contingency tables, forbidden positions and general nonbipartite graphs have different state spaces or moves. A theorem for arbitrary feasible binary margins is broad enough here, while its consequences for those other sampling questions must be assessed separately.

cards.title: An FPRAS for perfect matchings in general graphs
cards.formal: Does there exist a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for the number Z(G) of perfect matchings in every finite undirected simple graph G? More precisely, is there one randomized algorithm A and one polynomial p such that, for every explicitly encoded graph G and rational 0<ε<1, A halts within p(L,⌈1/ε⌉) bit operations and outputs a nonnegative rational Ẑ satisfying Pr[(1−ε)Z(G)≤Ẑ≤(1+ε)Z(G)]≥3/4, where L is the total binary input length?
cards.definitions: A matching is a set of edges with no shared endpoints. It is perfect if every vertex is incident to exactly one selected edge. Z(G) is the number of distinct such edge sets; edges and vertices are unweighted. The graph is specified by a labeled vertex set and its full edge list, without bipartiteness, density, degree, expansion or planarity promises. For an odd number of vertices Z(G)=0; for the empty graph Z(G)=1. The random bits are independent fair bits, all computational and output costs are counted, and the time bound holds for every random tape. When Z(G)=0, require output zero with probability one; this causes no loss of generality because existence of a perfect matching can be decided deterministically in polynomial time before approximation begins. The fixed success probability 3/4 can be amplified to 1−δ by independent repetitions and a median, with an O(log(1/δ)) multiplicative overhead. The same polynomial p must work for all graphs and all requested accuracies. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A canonical unresolved problem in approximate counting, separating efficient existence testing from estimating the number of solutions. It also controls the approximability of other counting and partition-function problems through reductions.

importance.reason: The major missing generalization of the permanent FPRAS, with an established obstruction to the direct Markov-chain approach and consequences beyond matchings.

progress.text: Jerrum–Sinclair give an FPRAS for the monomer–dimer partition function, which counts matchings of all sizes. This is not an unrestricted perfect-matching FPRAS.
Jerrum–Sinclair–Vigoda establish an FPRAS for nonnegative permanents, solving approximate perfect-matching counting in bipartite graphs.
Štefankovič–Vigoda–Wilmes prove slow mixing for general-graph extensions of the JSV approach and give algorithms based on bounded factor-critical structure.
The revised Fei–Goldberg–Lu paper retains general perfect-matching counting as an unresolved approximation class in its spin-system classification.
Chen–Vigoda–Yang improve the permanent FPRAS to O(r⁶ ε⁻² log⁵ r log(2/δ)) for r×r zero–one matrices. The graph remains bipartite.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The general-graph question remains open in the checked primary literature. The August 2026 improvement is a permanent algorithm for bipartite graphs. Slow mixing of the particular general-graph Markov chains does not establish impossibility of all FPRAS approaches.

context_blocks.text: Finding a perfect matching and estimating how many exist are different tasks. Edmonds’ algorithm handles existence and maximum cardinality in general graphs, whereas exact counting is #P-complete even in bipartite graphs. Approximation avoids asking for every digit of a potentially exponential count, but still requires a reliable multiplicative estimate. The 2018 paper of Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes places this gap at the center of general matching-counting research.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda resolve the bipartite case through an FPRAS for the permanent of any nonnegative matrix. A square bipartite adjacency matrix records allowed pairs between two fixed vertex classes; a permutation chooses one partner for every vertex. The algorithm combines a Markov chain on perfect and near-perfect matchings with simulated annealing and weights that balance different pairs of unmatched vertices.

Applying that theorem to the ordinary adjacency matrix of a nonbipartite graph does not count its perfect matchings. For example, K₄ has three perfect matchings, but its adjacency matrix has permanent nine: the latter also counts directed cycle-cover patterns. The corresponding general-graph quantity is a hafnian, a sum over partitions of the vertex set into unordered pairs. The distinction is combinatorial, not a matter of merely changing the matrix dimensions.

Counting all matchings is another solved neighboring problem: Jerrum and Sinclair give an FPRAS for the monomer–dimer partition function. The desired perfect matchings may form a very small fraction of that distribution. A disjoint union of k edges already has 2ᵏ matchings and just one perfect matching. Thus approximate uniform sampling from all matchings, followed by waiting for a perfect one, need not run in polynomial time. This example concerns that proposed reduction, not hardness of counting on the example graph.

Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes show that the straightforward extension of the JSV chain encounters exponential mixing bottlenecks on general graphs; changing weights based only on the unmatched-vertex pattern does not give a universal remedy. They also use the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition to obtain algorithms for structurally restricted graphs. A factor-critical component is one whose deletion of any one vertex leaves a perfect matching. Their parameter concerns the number of ears in such a component’s ear decomposition, not simply its vertex count.

The problem matters beyond matching counts themselves. Fei, Goldberg and Lu’s 2025 journal paper classifies approximation of several two-state spin-system partition functions. Some parameter settings are linked by approximation-preserving reductions to perfect-matching counting in general graphs, and the paper explicitly retains that task as a central open question. A resolution would therefore determine tractability for related counting models as well.

cards.context:
Finding a perfect matching and estimating how many exist are different tasks. Edmonds’ algorithm handles existence and maximum cardinality in general graphs, whereas exact counting is #P-complete even in bipartite graphs. Approximation avoids asking for every digit of a potentially exponential count, but still requires a reliable multiplicative estimate. The 2018 paper of Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes places this gap at the center of general matching-counting research.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda resolve the bipartite case through an FPRAS for the permanent of any nonnegative matrix. A square bipartite adjacency matrix records allowed pairs between two fixed vertex classes; a permutation chooses one partner for every vertex. The algorithm combines a Markov chain on perfect and near-perfect matchings with simulated annealing and weights that balance different pairs of unmatched vertices.

Applying that theorem to the ordinary adjacency matrix of a nonbipartite graph does not count its perfect matchings. For example, K₄ has three perfect matchings, but its adjacency matrix has permanent nine: the latter also counts directed cycle-cover patterns. The corresponding general-graph quantity is a hafnian, a sum over partitions of the vertex set into unordered pairs. The distinction is combinatorial, not a matter of merely changing the matrix dimensions.

Counting all matchings is another solved neighboring problem: Jerrum and Sinclair give an FPRAS for the monomer–dimer partition function. The desired perfect matchings may form a very small fraction of that distribution. A disjoint union of k edges already has 2ᵏ matchings and just one perfect matching. Their parameter concerns the number of ears in such a component’s ear decomposition, not simply its vertex count.

cards.title: Does #BIS admit an FPRAS?
cards.formal: Does there exist one probabilistic Turing algorithm A and one polynomial p such that, for every finite simple bipartite graph G and rational ε∈(0,1), A(G,ε) halts within p(L,⌈1/ε⌉) steps on every random tape and returns a nonnegative rational Ẑ with Pr[(1−ε)Z(G)≤Ẑ≤(1+ε)Z(G)]≥3/4? L is the full input bit length, including ε; Z(G) is the number of independent sets.
cards.definitions: The input lists the vertices, their bipartition U,V and all edges, with no loops or repeated edges; ε is supplied as a positive binary numerator and denominator. An independent set I⊆U∪V contains no edge’s two endpoints. Z(G) counts all such subsets, including ∅, so Z(G)≥1 and the empty graph has Z=1. The output is a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator representing Ẑ≥0. A uses independent fair coin bits, with no advice or oracle. All input reading, computation, random-bit access and output writing count toward the bound. The success probability is separately required on every input and is over A’s coins. The same program and polynomial work for all bipartitions, degrees, graph sizes and accuracies.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determines whether the canonical intermediate approximate-counting problem can be solved with a uniform polynomial-time randomized relative-error algorithm, with consequences for many equivalent counting and statistical-mechanics problems.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved boundary in approximate counting, with broad approximation-preserving consequences and a well-defined gap between FPRAS and hardness evidence.

context_blocks.text: #BIS asks for the number of independent sets in an arbitrary bipartite graph. Exact counting is already difficult, while approximate counting places the problem in a widely studied intermediate regime: it is a canonical complete problem for the class #RHΠ₁ under approximation-preserving reductions, and many spin-system and combinatorial counting problems are equivalent to it. The main unresolved issue is whether this intermediate status hides a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme.

The relative-error requirement matters when the graph has few independent sets as well as when it has exponentially many. The algorithm must work for every explicitly encoded graph and every requested accuracy, with no structural promise that would make local sampling mix rapidly. A polynomial bound in |V| alone, an additive approximation, or an algorithm whose polynomial degree depends on the graph family would be a different statement.

Several restricted classes do admit efficient approximation schemes. For example, results for almost every sufficiently regular bipartite graph and for dense regular bipartite graphs exploit expansion or spectral structure. These theorems demonstrate that the target is achievable on substantial subclasses, but they do not provide a worst-case FPRAS for arbitrary bipartite inputs.

The conjectured difficulty is deliberately weaker than #P-hardness of approximation. #BIS is believed not to have an FPRAS, yet it is also believed not to be NP-hard under the usual approximation-preserving reductions. Resolving the card would therefore locate a central intermediate point between problems with known FPRASes and problems with robust hardness barriers.

The earlier catalogue pointer TCS-6225 came from a paper on independent sets in random regular bipartite graphs and preserved only a truncated source excerpt. This card states the general #BIS question explicitly and keeps the restricted-family results as progress rather than treating them as a solution.

cards.title: A deterministic FPTAS for the nonnegative permanent
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that, for every explicitly given nonnegative rational n×n matrix A and every rational ε∈(0,1), outputs a rational Z satisfying (1−ε)per(A)≤Z≤(1+ε)per(A) in time polynomial in the input bit length and 1/ε?
cards.definitions: For n≥1, per(A)=Σ_{π∈S_n}∏_{i=1}^n A_{i,π(i)}, where S_n is the set of permutations of [n]. Each entry is represented by a nonnegative integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. Let L be the total binary description length of A and ε. There must be one fixed polynomial P such that the algorithm uses at most P(L,1/ε) bit operations on every input. Ordinary deterministic Turing computation is intended, with output bits and arithmetic costs counted; there are no random bits, nonuniform advice, counting oracles or exact-real unit-cost operations. No density, expansion, lower-bound-on-positive-entries, bounded-degree or matrix-scaling promise is imposed. Zero entries are allowed. If per(A)=0, the algorithm must return Z=0 exactly. This zero case is decidable in polynomial time by checking whether the bipartite support graph has a perfect matching. FPTAS means fully polynomial-time approximation scheme: the running-time exponent must be independent of ε, and the error is relative to per(A), not additive relative to n!, a matrix norm, or another normalization.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such a deterministic approximation scheme or prove that none exists. A randomized FPRAS does not settle the deterministic question. An approximation within a factor depending superconstantly on n, or a scheme with running time n^{g(1/ε)}, does not meet the stated guarantee. Exact #P-hardness alone is not a refutation, since using exponentially small ε is allowed to take exponential time under the FPTAS bound.
cards.why: A landmark derandomization problem: match the accuracy and efficiency of the permanent FPRAS using deterministic computation on every nonnegative rational matrix.

importance.reason: One of the central explicit tests of derandomization in approximate counting, with broad connections to matchings, sampling, convex optimization and correlation decay.

context_blocks.text: For a zero–one matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings in its bipartite support graph: rows and columns are the two vertex classes, and a permutation chooses one allowed partner for every row. With nonnegative weights it sums the products of edge weights over these matchings. Finding one perfect matching is efficient, but estimating how much total weight all perfect matchings contribute is a different task.

Unlike the determinant, the permanent has no alternating signs in its permutation sum. Nonnegativity makes multiplicative approximation meaningful even when the total is very small. It also makes zero detection easy: a positive permanent is equivalent to existence of a perfect matching using positive entries. The hard part is accurate quantitative estimation on positive instances, not distinguishing an arbitrary exponentially tiny value from zero by floating-point tolerance.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda provide a randomized fully polynomial approximation scheme for every nonnegative matrix. Their method combines weighted perfect and near-perfect matchings, sampling and simulated annealing. Thus a solution need not discover that approximate counting is possible; it must remove randomness while retaining arbitrary relative accuracy and polynomial dependence on the requested inverse accuracy.

The randomized side continues to improve. Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s August 2026 preprint reduces the reported running time for zero–one matrices to O(n⁶ log⁵ n) when the relative accuracy and success probability are fixed, with an extension to general nonnegative matrices. The better analysis concerns a restricted Poincaré inequality for the Markov chain. It remains a sampling-based randomized algorithm.

A major deterministic approach is the Bethe permanent, obtained from a variational optimization over doubly stochastic matrices. Anari and Rezaei prove that it lower-bounds the permanent and loses at most a factor 2^{n/2}. This factor is attained on block-diagonal matrices built from two-by-two all-ones blocks. The tight example limits the unmodified Bethe estimate, rather than proving that every deterministic approximation algorithm must lose that much.

In late August 2026, Anari and independently Narang and Perkins go beyond the canonical Bethe estimate. Both approaches exploit structure near the bad two-by-two blocks and achieve a factor c^n for some absolute c<√2. This improves the exponential base. A fixed positive base above one, however, still gives an error factor growing exponentially with the matrix dimension.

The September 9 preprint of Kudria, Luo and Majid improves the general deterministic polynomial-time guarantee to exp(O(n(log log n)²/log n))=exp(o(n)). Its algorithm uses convex optimization of weighted matching sums, together with deterministic correlation-decay estimates. The theorem explicitly handles arbitrary nonnegative rational matrices in the bit model, so it applies to this card’s input class. Its approximation factor is still much larger than 1+ε.

There is a useful amplification threshold. Make a block-diagonal matrix containing r copies of A; its permanent is per(A)^r. If a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm approximated an N by N permanent within exp(O(N^{1−γ})) for one fixed γ>0, applying it at N=rn and taking an rth root would reduce the logarithmic error to O(n^{1−γ}/r^γ). Polynomially many copies in n and 1/ε would then suffice for an FPTAS.

The September theorem’s logarithmic saving does not cross that threshold: polynomially many copies increase log(rn) by only a constant-factor scale, leaving a large logarithmic error after root extraction. Consequently, subexponential approximation and arbitrary relative accuracy remain distinct milestones. A solution would remove one of the most prominent uses of randomness in approximate counting while clarifying how much global matching information deterministic optimization can recover.

cards.title: Can all vertices of a rational polytope be enumerated in output-polynomial time?
cards.formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and a polynomial p such that, for every rational matrix M and rational vector b with P={x∈R^d:Mx≤b} bounded, A lists each vertex of P exactly once and halts within p(L+S) bit operations, where L is the binary input length and S is the total binary length of the required vertex list? The dimension d is part of the input.
cards.definitions: The input specifies integers m,d≥1, M∈Q^(m×d), and b∈Q^m. Every rational is written as a reduced signed integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary, with delimiters; L includes this entire explicit representation. P may be empty or lower-dimensional, and redundant inequalities and degeneracy are allowed. A vertex is an extreme point: v∈P such that v=(x+y)/2 with x,y∈P implies x=y=v. Every vertex is rational. The output is a finite list in arbitrary order of these vectors, with each coordinate in the same reduced rational encoding, followed by an end marker. S includes separators and the end marker; it is determined independently of the algorithm, so padding or duplicate outputs cannot enlarge the permitted bound. The empty polytope has an empty vertex list. The bound concerns total running time, including writing the output, without a polynomial-delay or polynomial-workspace requirement. Correctness and the bound are required on the bounded-polyhedron promise; behavior outside that promise is immaterial.

context_blocks.text: A finite system of inequalities describes a convex region implicitly, while a vertex list describes its extremal feasible points explicitly. Linear programming can optimize one linear objective without producing that list. Enumerating the list asks whether the entire conversion can be performed with only polynomial overhead relative to the information that must actually be returned.

The number of vertices can be exponential in the input length, so a running-time bound polynomial in the input alone would be inappropriate. Output-polynomial time allows that unavoidable cost. It still excludes an algorithm that examines exponentially many intermediate objects when the final list is short. Degeneracy is particularly relevant because many collections of tight inequalities can describe the same vertex.

Reimers and Stougie explicitly identify total-polynomial vertex enumeration for bounded polyhedra as a longstanding open question. They obtain such an algorithm under a bounded branch-width condition. Their paper also distinguishes the general unbounded-polyhedron problem, for which output-polynomial enumeration would imply P=NP. That hardness statement does not resolve the bounded target here.

Dong, Fan, Xiong and Zeng study vertices of hyperplane arrangements. An arrangement includes intersections that may lie outside the feasible region selected by a system of inequalities. Consequently, an output-sensitive bound for the entire arrangement is measured against a different output and does not establish the required bound in the number of vertices of this polytope.

This card adds geometric enumeration to a category that already contains counting and hypergraph-transversal questions. Its target is the exact finite output of an algorithm in variable dimension. Neither approximate vertices nor a fast method restricted to simple polytopes meets that target.

cards.title: Are all Boolean log-supermodular counting CSPs #BIS-easy?
cards.formal: For every fixed finite family F of functions f:{0,1}^{r_f}→ℚ_{≥0} satisfying f(x∨y)f(x∧y)≥f(x)f(y) for all x,y, is #CSP(F) approximation-preserving reducible to #BIS?
cards.definitions: Arity r_f is a nonnegative integer fixed with f; ∨ and ∧ act coordinatewise. A #CSP(F) instance consists of finitely many Boolean variables and a list of constraints, each naming a function in F and an ordered tuple of variables of its arity; repeats in a tuple are permitted. Its value Z is the sum over all Boolean assignments of the product of all constraint values. Function tables are fixed nonnegative rationals, not part of the instance. #BIS counts all independent vertex sets of a finite simple bipartite graph. An approximation-preserving reduction is a randomized oracle algorithm which, on an instance I and rational ε∈(0,1), returns a relative (1±ε) estimate of Z with probability at least 3/4 using time polynomial in |I| and 1/ε. Its oracle calls request relative approximations to #BIS with inverse tolerances polynomially bounded in |I| and 1/ε. Oracle failure probabilities may be reduced to an inverse polynomial by independent repetitions; the reduction’s overall correctness guarantee includes them. If Z=0, a valid relative estimate is exactly zero. Reduction polynomials may depend on the fixed family F. The oracle is an approximation oracle, not exact counting.

context_blocks.text: Exact finite-domain counting CSPs already have major dichotomy theorems. Approximate counting has a different landscape, and log-supermodularity is one of its central boundaries. This question asks whether that whole Boolean region reduces to the benchmark problem #BIS.

Some log-supermodular functions cannot be represented by the standard implication-and-unary gadgets. That algebraic obstruction does not refute an approximation-preserving reduction, which is a more general notion. The target is this computational gap, not a claim that every counting problem has an established three-way classification.

cards.definitions: H=([n],E), n≥0, is supplied as the explicit vertex list and a finite list of edges e⊆[n], each edge an increasing list of binary vertex identifiers. Repeated edges have no effect. L(H) is the bit length of this input including delimiters. A transversal is a set T⊆[n] intersecting every e∈E; it is inclusion-minimal when no proper subset has this property. Output each such T as an increasing list of its binary vertex identifiers with a delimiter, in arbitrary order; no duplicate, nonminimal or incomplete output is allowed. L_out(H) is the sum of the bit lengths of these records, counting one delimiter even for T=∅. If E is empty, the unique minimal transversal is ∅. If E contains ∅, there is no transversal and L_out=0. Time includes all computation, output and termination detection. The polynomial and algorithm are independent of n, E, edge size and output size; there is no separate delay or workspace bound, advice, oracle or randomization. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.title: Are splay trees dynamically optimal?
cards.formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let OPT(X) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree T₀ and every X, $\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)$? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.

context_blocks.text: A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost Θ(n), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by O((OPT(X)+n) log log n · log² log log n). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

cards.why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.
cards.definitions: Keys are [n]={1,…,n}, n≥1, ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence X∈[n]*, cost_splay(X;T₀) is the sum of these costs starting from T₀. A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. OPT(X) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.

progress.text: Splaying has logarithmic amortized access cost and stronger guarantees for useful special patterns. These do not establish competitiveness against an arbitrary changing offline tree.
Tango trees give an online BST with an $O(\log\log n)$ competitive ratio. This result is for a different data structure and does not settle splaying.
The preprint proves $O((\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)$ total splay cost. Theorem 1 includes the initialization term explicitly. Constant competitiveness remains the target.

cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer k≥2 and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions F_n on an n-word database and a k⌈log₂ n⌉-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity t*F(n), with word size ⌈4log₂ n⌉ bits and n⌈log₂ n⌉² memory cells, satisfies t*F(n)/log₂ n→∞ as n→∞?
cards.definitions: For each integer n≥2 put w=⌈4log₂ n⌉ and s=n⌈log₂ n⌉². A database is D∈({0,1}^w)^n, a query is q∈{0,1}^{k⌈log₂ n⌉}, and F_n(D,q)∈{0,1}. Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes F_n(D,q), given (1^n,D,q), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map E_n into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output F_n(D,q) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through E_n(D). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define t*F(n) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real B>0 there is N such that t*F(n)>B log₂ n for every n≥N. Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite B>0 such that t*F(n)≤B log₂ n for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an O(log n) bound for all sufficiently large n.
cards.why: A central unconditional lower-bound bottleneck for data structures: establish that a short, explicitly defined static query fundamentally needs more than logarithmically many memory accesses despite unrestricted preprocessing.

The STOC 2026 paper retains the broader static barrier as Open Problem 1.1. context_blocks.text: A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least n² possible queries, while the stored representation has only O(n log³ n) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is O(log n), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to Θ(log n)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is Ω(min{log(m/s), n/log s}) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most O(log n). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further Ω((log n/log log n)²) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.

cards.title: Can a static dictionary be built deterministically in linear time?
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every fixed integer d≥1 there are uniform deterministic construction and query programs A_d,Q_d and a constant C_d≥1 such that, for every n≥2, every word length ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉≤w≤d⌈log₂(n+1)⌉, and every n-record input with distinct w-bit integer keys and w-bit values, A_d builds a static dictionary in at most C_d n operations and C_d n words of total space, and Q_d answers every membership-and-value query in at most C_d operations.
cards.why: Exact constant-time lookup is a basic component of many larger data structures. The unresolved cost is obtaining the representation deterministically in optimal time, so a resolution would settle whether randomness is essential to this combination of construction, storage and lookup guarantees.
cards.status_note: The primary dictionary results, later applications and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No complete resolution of the specified logarithmic-word deterministic construction target was found. The accessible 2025 draft Slightly more practical deterministic static dictionaries was also inspected; it contains unfinished statements and does not claim the required linear construction, so it is not used to certify a new bound.

cards.definitions: The universe is U_w={0,…,2ʷ−1}. An input is a list of n pairs (x_i,v_i)∈U_w×U_w with pairwise distinct x_i and arbitrary v_i; the input order is unrestricted. On query q∈U_w the output is (1,v_i) if q=x_i and (0,0) if q is absent. The stored set and values do not change after construction. The machine is a sequential word RAM with w-bit registers and cells. The primitive unit-cost instructions are memory reads and writes, copies, comparisons, conditional branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication returning the full product in two words, integer quotient and remainder of two words with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least w returns zero; otherwise shifted-out bits are discarded. Addresses may occupy a fixed number of words, and all operations computing them are charged. Programs have finitely many instructions and constants, may receive n and w, and contain no input-size or word-size advice, random instruction, free table or special hashing primitive. Every table, parameter computation, memory initialization and output write performed by construction counts toward its time; input storage, the resulting dictionary and temporary storage count toward its space. Query reads the constructed representation and may use temporary workspace, with every operation charged; all retained information about the input is in the counted representation. The query must be correct on every q, including absent keys. Programs and constants may depend on d but not on n, w, the input or query. This spells out the saved w=Θ(log n) convention as a claim for every fixed polynomial-size universe; Pagh’s broader arbitrary-word-length formulation is not asserted equivalent here.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition with deterministic algorithms meeting all three bounds for every fixed d, or disprove it for at least one fixed d. The negation says that no pair of admissible correct programs has simultaneously linear worst-case construction time, linear total space and constant worst-case query time for all inputs in that word-length range. Failure of a particular hash family, an average-input lower bound, or a lower bound in a comparison-only model is not that negation.

context_blocks.text: A dictionary is an exact lookup table for a sparse set of keys. For example, records (12,5), (47,9) and (103,2) require the answers 9 on key 47 and absent on key 48. The values need not be unique. The problem is to prepare a representation in time proportional to the number of records and then answer every lookup in a bounded number of machine steps, regardless of whether the key is present.

Direct addressing uses the key itself as an array index. This achieves constant lookup time, but an array for a universe of n² possible keys occupies n² cells even if only n keys are present. Such space is outside the target. At the opposite extreme, keeping the keys in sorted order uses linear space but ordinary binary search needs logarithmically many comparisons. These examples show why construction, storage and query time must be required simultaneously.

Randomized perfect hashing already gives linear expected construction time, linear storage and constant worst-case lookup time. The randomness concerns finding a suitable representation during construction; once a valid dictionary has been built, lookup can be exact and have a worst-case bound. Thus the open issue is not whether every query can avoid probabilistic errors, but whether the construction time can be bounded linearly without any random choices.

Pagh obtained deterministic O(n log n) construction for logarithmic-size words. Ružić subsequently related construction cost to integer sorting with only a log log n overhead. The latter is a much smaller overhead, but it still grows with n. The source question asks for its complete removal while retaining the other two guarantees. A representation whose existence is known but whose parameters take longer to find does not meet the construction requirement.

The dependence on word length matters even when keys occupy one machine word. Here a fixed polynomial-size universe is intended: the constant relating w to log n is fixed before the inputs vary. Constants in the guarantees may depend on that fixed bound. This is the logarithmic-word version already selected for this card; it does not silently claim a solution for word lengths growing faster than log n.

Uniformity also matters. Earlier dictionary results sometimes supplied word-size-dependent constants at no construction cost. The present formulation charges for computing every table and parameter that is not part of a fixed program. A one-time computation on a particular physical machine cannot disappear from an asymptotic bound that covers arbitrarily large inputs.

The dependency remains visible in modern applications. The 2024 internal-pattern-matching paper uses constant-time deterministic dictionaries with a general O(m(log log m)²) construction bound for a dictionary of size m, and treats very small dictionaries separately. The surrounding text length can be much larger than m, so that application must not be read as fixing word length to Θ(log m). Kosolobov’s 2026 compressed index likewise records a slowdown when dictionary randomness is removed.

These applications explain the scientific stakes: a basic lookup operation can determine whether a larger construction remains deterministic within its intended time bound. The 2026 index is evidence that the issue remains useful, rather than a theorem resolving this static linear-construction question.

cards.title: Do splay trees support deque operations in constant amortized time?
cards.formal: Start from an arbitrary binary search tree containing $n$ ordered keys, and perform $m$ legal double-ended queue operations. Insert-min creates a new minimum as the root with the old tree as its right child; insert-max is symmetric. Delete-min splays the minimum to the root, removes it, and keeps its right subtree; delete-max is symmetric. Is the total number of primitive pointer operations and rotations always $O(n+m)$, with a universal constant? This is Tarjan’s deque conjecture for the specified splay implementation.
cards.why: I include this because it tests whether one general-purpose adaptive representation can recognize a workload whose optimal cost is linear. The remaining gap is tiny numerically but significant mathematically: a proof would explain why expensive local restructuring cannot accumulate across arbitrary alternations of the two ends.
cards.definitions: Splaying uses the standard zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rules. Deletions are allowed only on a nonempty tree, and an inserted key must be outside the current key range at the specified end. Amortized cost is a bound on the total sequence, not a worst-case guarantee for each deletion. The initial tree may have any shape.

progress.text: Pettie proves $O((n+m)\alpha^*(n+m))$ total cost, where $\alpha^*$ counts how many iterations of the inverse-Ackermann function reduce the argument to a constant.
Levy and Tarjan connect the deque conjecture to a subsequence property sufficient for dynamic optimality. This provides a structural route to a proof, not the required linear bound itself.
The new analysis of splay competitiveness still describes the deque guarantee as nearly constant per operation. Its general search bound does not supply constant amortized deque cost.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July 2026 splay result. The conjecture asks for linear total cost under insertions and deletions at either end.

context_blocks.text: A deque allows insertion and deletion at either end of a sequence. A linked representation can implement this abstract interface in constant time per operation. The conjecture concerns what happens when the same interface is implemented by a self-adjusting search tree: it asks whether the tree automatically achieves the linear total cost available for this restricted workload.

Deleting the minimum of a long left spine can require many rotations in a single operation. That does not disprove the conjecture, because the initial tree contributes an additive budget proportional to its size. The real difficulty is to understand whether alternating insertions and deletions at opposite ends can repeatedly rebuild expensive configurations.

For a concrete contrast, deleting keys in increasing order is a sequential-access pattern. A deque workload can switch ends after every operation and introduce new extreme keys between deletions. A bound for one monotone scan therefore does not immediately control this more flexible sequence.

The known total bound has an iterated inverse-Ackermann factor, which grows extraordinarily slowly but is asymptotically unbounded. Removing it would answer a structural question about how rotations reuse earlier work. This is a focused subproblem of the broader study of splaying, with updates included explicitly rather than only searches.

cards.title: Do pure pairing heaps support O(log log n) amortized decrease-key?
cards.formal: For the pure pairing heap defined below, is there a universal constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations starting with empty heaps costs at most $C[M+D(1+\log N)+K(1+\log\log(N+2))]$? Here D counts delete-min operations, K counts decrease-key operations, and $N\ge2$ is the maximum of 2 and the total number of live items across all heaps at any moment. The allowed operations are make-heap, insert, find-min, meld, decrease-key, and delete-min. Count comparisons and pointer-machine steps; keys are distinct opaque values in a totally ordered set, compared at unit cost. Handles to the affected items and heaps are supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove this total-cost bound for the specified algorithm, or construct legal operation sequences for which its ratio to the displayed budget is unbounded. Changing the heap algorithm or obtaining the bound only for a different self-adjusting heap does not establish a positive answer.
cards.definitions: A heap is one rooted heap-ordered tree whose child lists are ordered from left to right. Linking two roots compares their keys and makes the larger root the leftmost child of the smaller; cut removes a node with its subtree from its parent in constant time. Store O(1) pointers per item, with doubly linked child lists. Make-heap creates an empty tree; find-min returns its root; insert links a singleton to the root; meld links the roots and destroys the old heap handles. Decrease-key changes the supplied key and, if its node is not the root, cuts that node and links its subtree with the remaining root. Delete-min removes the root and scans its children left to right, linking disjoint adjacent pairs; an unpaired last child remains. Winners keep their positions in the root list. Identify its minimum-key remaining root v, remove v from that list, and prepend all other remaining roots in their existing order to the child list of v. The resulting tree is the heap. Use the ordinary constant-time list splice, rather than doing an additional recursive linking pass. All loops, comparisons, pointer accesses, and writes are charged. Logarithms have base two.
cards.why: This is a precise opportunity to separate an analysis gap from a structural limitation of a simple data structure. Priority-queue costs propagate into graph algorithms, and the problem tests how little explicit balancing information is sufficient for optimal amortized behavior.

progress.text: Iacono and Özkan prove an Omega(log log n) decrease-key lower bound in the pure heap model under logarithmic extract-min bounds. The model name refers to a class, not specifically the 2026 data structure.

Sinnamon and Tarjan establish optimal logarithmic-logarithmic decrease-key bounds for slim and smooth heaps, with a further log log log n factor for multipass pairing heaps. The journal version appeared in 2025.

Tarjan and Xu introduce pure pairing heaps and bound decrease-key by O(log log n times log log log n), retaining O(log n) delete-min and O(1) insert/meld amortized bounds. Section 10 explicitly leaves the remaining factor open.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July 2026 primary preprint. The displayed bound uses the maximum live population, while the source also develops finer bounds that omit items never deleted. This card fixes one algorithm and one total-cost target.

context_blocks.text: A decrease-key call changes an item that is already present. It may execute only a few pointer operations immediately, yet the structural disorder it creates can make later deletions more expensive. Its amortized cost measures this delayed effect. Counting only the instructions inside the decrease-key procedure would miss the question entirely.

The pure pairing heap simplifies deletion by pairing neighboring roots once and then attaching all survivors beneath the smallest survivor. It does not maintain a rank or balance invariant. The desired estimate asks whether this sparse restructuring still prevents expensive configurations from being recreated too often.

The operation budgets must be considered together. A sorting sequence already forces substantial comparison work when many minima are deleted, so the logarithmic delete-min allowance is intentional. The unresolved issue is how much additional work to attribute to key decreases while keeping insertions and melds cheap. Using the maximum live population N makes that accounting explicit for a whole finite sequence.

Other self-adjusting heaps already attain the desired decrease-key order. This makes the remaining gap an informative algorithm-analysis problem: is the simpler rule equally efficient, or does its exact restructuring lose something asymptotically? A bound for slim or smooth heaps does not answer this question about pure pairing heaps.

cards.title: Polynomial-sample worst-case trace reconstruction
cards.formal: For every fixed deletion probability δ∈(0,1), is there a constant C_δ≥1 and K_δ≥1 such that every unknown n-bit string can be reconstructed exactly with probability at least 2/3 from at most K_δ n^{C_δ} independent deletion traces, for every n≥2?
cards.definitions: For x∈{0,1}^n, a deletion trace is generated by independently retaining each input bit with probability 1−δ and concatenating the retained bits in their original order. Let μ_{x,δ} be its probability distribution on ⋃_{k=0}^n{0,1}^k. Different traces use independent deletion masks. The estimator is given n, δ and m independent samples from μ_{x,δ}; it receives neither deletion positions nor direct access to x. Its output is an element of {0,1}^n, and success means equality to the entire original string. One estimator for the given n and δ must succeed for every x with probability at least 2/3 over the traces and any internal randomness. There is no restriction on processing time, storage, description length or computation between observations: this card asks an information-theoretic sample-complexity question. Formally, let N_δ(n) be the smallest integer m for which such an estimator exists. The target is N_δ(n)≤K_δ n^{C_δ} for every n≥2. The constants may depend on δ but not on n or x. The string is adversarially chosen and has no codebook, sparsity, separation, randomness or other structural promise. Traces are ordinary linear subsequences without cyclic shifts.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A fundamental question about how much information random subsequences preserve: can every string be identified from polynomially many observations despite completely hidden alignment?

cards.status_note: The July 2026 quasipolynomial sample theorem supersedes the saved 2025 general upper frontier but does not give polynomially many traces. The best unrestricted lower bound cited remains polynomial; circular and local-SQ bounds concern different models. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

There is an immediate exponential upper bound: with probability (1−δ)^n a trace suffers no deletions and reveals the entire string. After sufficiently many samples, such a length-n trace appears with high probability. The challenge is to extract the same information from much shorter typical traces without waiting for this rare event. Their lengths are observable, so the no-deletion event is recognizable.

Lower bounds can focus on two carefully selected strings whose trace distributions are extremely close. If even this binary hypothesis test needs many samples, reconstructing an arbitrary string cannot need fewer. Chase gives a lower bound of Ω(n^{3/2}/log⁷ n) for fixed deletion probability. This is a substantial obstruction to near-linear reconstruction, but it remains polynomial and is therefore consistent with the target.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses exp(Õ(n^{1/5})) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint proves a quasipolynomial sample upper bound, including every fixed positive retention probability. Its theorem bounds the number of traces by exp(p^{−7/3}(log₂ n)^c) for an absolute constant c, where p=1−δ. The strategy uses global statistics involving polylogarithmically many trace positions. It improves the upper frontier considerably while still leaving a gap to a fixed polynomial in n.

The same paper explicitly separates sample complexity from running time. Maximum-likelihood reconstruction can reuse these traces while comparing exponentially many candidate strings, whereas distinguishing two supplied candidates can be implemented much faster. The quasipolynomial sample theorem does not provide quasipolynomial time for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string. Since the current card imposes no time limit, this distinction does not weaken the sample result.

The change in statistics matters. A local statistical-query procedure learns only approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that model, nearly matching the older subexponential algorithm. Those lower bounds do not apply to unrestricted use of individual traces or to statistics involving widely separated positions. Thus the new global approach does not contradict the local-query barrier.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that O(n log n) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly n⁵ is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.
